articles.title: ASRA NOMANI: El-Sayed glides into role as rock star of the hard left's red-green alliance
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed appeared at an Arab America Foundation summit where CodePink activists and pro-Palestinian organizers revealed the coalition behind him.
articles.body: CHANTILLY, Va. — Three days after Abdul El-Sayed won a historic election as America's first Muslim senator, a driver navigating a black luxury GMC Yukon Denali SUV pulled into a parking space beside a side security entrance of an upscale Marriott conference center here in this suburb of Washington, D.C., at 7:39 p.m. on Friday. A man jumped out of the front passenger seat and opened the rear door, from which El-Sayed emerged for an appearance at the Arab America Foundation's "CONNECT Empowerment Summit," hosted by the 501(c)(3) nonprofit whose leaders had supported his election. As the man extended an arm to shield El-Sayed, the senator-elect dipped out of the SUV, slipping on a jacket as he climbed the steps toward the entrance. The Democratic Party's newly minted rock star had arrived, in more ways than one. ABDUL EL-SAYED DELIVERS MAJOR BLOW TO GOP IN MICHIGAN AFTER BRUISING SENATE RACE The ensuing 45 minutes offered a window into some of the activists, organizations, political rhetoric and cultural forces surrounding the El-Sayed's dramatic rise, buoyed by an increasingly powerful coalition that includes many disaffected Democrats, but also outright Islamists and communists in an unlikely alliance. Inside, Medea Benjamin, co-founder of CodePink, a far-left nonprofit, paced in the hallway in a fuchsia tunic over leggings and white boots. CodePink is a pro-communist, pro-China nonprofit funded by Neville Roy Singham, an American-born, Shanghai-based tycoon whose financing of left-wing nonprofits has drawn congressional and prosecutorial scrutiny. CodePink's other co-founder, Jodie Evans, is married to Singham. Nearby, Benjamin's husband and fellow CodePink activist, Tighe Barry, wore a traditional Chinese jacket under a khaki Mao-style cap emblazoned with a five-point star associated with communist iconography. He carried a backpack patterned with a keffiyeh pattern and watermelons, symbols adopted by pro-Palestinian activists. Benjamin and Barry weren't political outliers in El-Sayed's orbit. His political rise has been supported by prominent anti-Israel activists including Linda Sarsour and left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, who has called Hamas "1,000 times better" than Israel, a remark he later described as intentionally provocative. Friday night provided a firsthand view of another part of that coalition. They were among activists and representatives of organizations from different ideological traditions that have converged around El-Sayed — part of what Fox News Digital has examined as a "red-green" network linking elements of the socialist and communist hard-left with Muslim and Arab advocacy organizations. The gathering itself didn't fit neatly into a fundamentalist religious mold, amid questions about Islamism, or political Islam, and the Muslim Brotherhood that have followed El-Sayed. He has denied being a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, although his family reportedly has ties to the organization and he himself has written favorably about the organization's leaders. Women danced and sang with bare shoulders and flowing hair, underscoring the secular and openly cultural character of much of the celebration. A table for Jinba Village and School outside Hebron in the West Bank displayed a flyer reading, "End Settler Outposts: Make Palestinian Villages Safe. Email Congress." Another table offered keffiyehs with designs replacing the traditional fishbone pattern with the outlines of Palestinian territory. Along the far corner of the ballroom, a collection of gifts for a fundraiser included a handcrafted wooden "silhouette of Palestine, painted in the iconic colors of the Palestinian flag" by artist Hasan Munem. Opening bid: $100. ABDUL EL-SAYED'S ALLEGED FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SURFACE AFTER DENYING ANY LINK DURING NBC INTERVIEW Benjamin eventually took a seat beside Hazami Barmada, a prominent Syrian American anti-Israel activist who has deployed political theater and demonstrations across Virginia, Maryland and Washington, D.C., storming the offices of Palantir Technologies, Lockheed-Martin and PETA, the animal rights advocates, and confronting Biden and Trump administration officials to cut ties with Israel. Barmada wore a keffiyeh over her hair like a turban. Benjamin, Barry and Barmada declined to answer questions from Fox News Digital.Their presence put figures from different wings of the political coalition around El-Sayed in the same room: activists from the socialist, pro-communist Left alongside Arab, Muslim and pro-Palestinian activists and organizations that supported his candidacy. Fox News Digital has tracked the intersection of those movements as a "red-green" network — the "red" referring to socialist and communist organizations and "green" to Muslim and Arab political organizations. The groups don't share a single ideology or formal organizational structure but have converged around causes including opposition to Israel and U.S. foreign policy. Friday night, those relationships weren't nodes on an organizational chart. They were in the room. Co-founders Warren David and Dr. Amal David started the Arab America Foundation as an educational and cultural organization dedicated to promoting Arab heritage and connecting and empowering Arab Americans nationwide. Now they were waiting to greet the country's first Muslim senator. The foundation describes itself as nonpartisan, but political participation features prominently in its programming. The next morning, the summit's "Leading from the Front," included Abbas Alawieh and Layla Elabed, co-chairs of the Uncommitted National Movement, which organized Democratic voters in 2024 to cast "uncommitted" ballots in protest of the Biden administration's policies toward Israel and the war in Gaza. El-Sayed supported the Uncommitted effort. Also on the roster was Anas Shallal, CEO of the Washington, D.C., restaurant and bookstore, Bus Boys and Poets, which has hosted events involving left-wing organizations, including groups in the Singham network such as CodePink, on issues ranging from Israel and the Trump administration and Israel to Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The summit also included Arab American Institute founder James Zogby among dozens of artists, musicians and business, government and community leaders. But Friday night, El-Sayed was the celebrity guest. ‘DESTROYING THE AMERICAN WAY OF LIFE’: EL-SAYED’S POLITICAL ORBIT COMPLICATES EFFORT TO MODERATE HIS IMAGE Benjamin, Barry and Barmada rushed into one hallway before being directed back toward another as organizers and supporters tried to determine where El-Sayed would enter. Supporters eventually gathered near a doorway beside displays depicting Israel and the Palestinian territories as a single state of Palestine. At 7:51 p.m., El-Sayed finally appeared through a side door, beaming. The ballroom erupted in zaghrouta, high-pitched celebratory ululations traditionally heard at Arab weddings. In his khaki Mao-style cap, Barry filmed the arriving senator-elect on his phone, as El-Sayed passed Benjamin and Barmada, then then swung his camera toward Benjamin, who pumped her hands near her shoulders in celebration. Supporters cheered as El-Sayed made his way onto the stage. Before the senator-elect even began his remarks, another office entered the conversation: the presidency. Emcee Ameera David, a journalist and daughter of the co-founders, told the audience that her seven-year-old Egyptian American son had awakened Wednesday morning after El-Sayed's victory and asked her, "Mom, can he run for president?" "Yeah!" someone shouted as the room exploded in cheers and applause. "To which I happily replied, 'Yes he can,'" David continued. "And you can, too." El-Sayed smiled. REAGAN-ERA OFFICIAL WARNS ‘RED-GREEN ALLIANCE’ HAS SHARED GOAL OF ‘DESTROYING’ AMERICA The presidential talk came just hours after El-Sayed had registered Habibi PAC with the Federal Election Commission, according to records, defining it as a leadership PAC separate from his principal campaign committee. The committee gives the incoming senator a vehicle to raise money and make contributions to other candidates and political committees. The timing put the new committee into the backdrop of a celebration where some supporters were already discussing El-Sayed's political future beyond the Senate. The PAC's name borrowed the Arabic term of endearment that El-Sayed had propelled into national political conversation during his election-night victory speech. With a wry smile, El-Sayed addressed Vice President JD Vance as "JD, habibi," noting that Vance would be called upon to swear him into the Senate in January. In just three days, "Habibi" had gone from an election-night line to the name of a federal political committee. Then came a more explicit description of the political "movement" surrounding El-Sayed from the chairman of the organization hosting him. At 7:53 p.m., Arab America Foundation Chair Issam Andoni, a local tech entrepreneur whom the emcee had introduced as a "long time supporter of El-Sayed, stepped forward with a scarf over his shoulders designed with the keffiyeh fishbone pattern and the word "PALESTINE." Andoni denounced Trump and Republicans and lauded El-Sayed's success over what he called the "Democrat Zionist." "But Habibi Abdul," he said, to laughter and applause, "you destroyed them all." El-Sayed smiled quietly. "You destroyed AIPAC twice," Andoni continued, referring to the primary and the general election. "He showed them a steel backbone," he told the audience. "That steel backbone they never saw before. And that steel backbone is what created a movement behind him." Andoni predicted, "And I'm sure that movement, it's going to grow and grow and grow. And it's going to connect with other movements." "And with the sumud," the Arabic word for "steadfastness," "of our people in Gaza, West Bank and Lebanon, I'm sure we'll see a free Palestine from the river to the sea." QUIET PART OUT LOUD: ANTI-ISRAEL MOBS WANT ONE STATE CALLED 'PALESTINE,' ERASING ISRAEL"Palestine will be free," a woman shouted. Al-Sayed listened quietly, his hands clasped in front of him. As the crowd erupted in applause and cheers, Andoni continued, "A free Palestine, free Palestine from the river to the sea. Free from occupation. Free from Zionists. And free from corruption. And free from apartheid." The phrase "from the river to the sea" is fiercely contested. Supporters describe it as a call for Palestinian "freedom," while critics, including many Jewish organizations, interpret it as an anti-Semitic call for the elimination of Israel as a Jewish state from the Jordan River and Mediterranean Sea. The implications became less theoretical when Fox News Digital later asked people at the gathering what Palestinian freedom meant to them. Abdullah Abualrub, Virginia state organizer for the Council on American-Islamic Relations, or CAIR, was manning the organization's table at the summit. Speaking explicitly in his personal capacity, Abualrub told Fox News Digital he supported a Palestinian right of return. "I believe that all Palestinians should have a right to return to their country," he said, describing his own family as part of the Palestinian diaspora. Asked about Palestinians returning to territory within modern-day Israel and receiving equal political rights, Abualrub said the "dream is that everyone lives in peace" and that Jewish people "who are following the law" should be "free to live wherever they want." Experts told Fox News Digital that, under the rubric of a core set of principles, called "thawabet," adopted by the Palestinian national movement decades ago, a broader political program includes a one-state solution "free from Zionists," and the right of return to modern-day Israel for Palestinians displaced during the creation of the state of Israel and their descendants. El-Sayed's spokeswoman didn't respond to a request for comment on his position on a one-state solution with a "right of return" for Palestinians to Israel. A short embrace followed Andoni's introduction, and then El-Sayed stepped to the microphone. "My name is Abdul-Rehman Mohammed El-Sayed," he said to applause and laughter. "And I'm honored to be the next United States senator from the great state of Michigan," the "capital of Arab America." He walked through stories that have become part of his public narrative: how his name contains sounds Americans struggle to pronounce, how his grandmother once told him each of his cousins possessed some quality superior to his and how he shortened Abdul-Rahman to Abdul at a time when singer Paula Abdul and basketball legend Kareem Abdul-Jabbar made the name familiar to Americans. Six minutes later, at 7:59 p.m., a woman, Rima Ayyash, rose from the front row and let out the high-pitched celebratory ululations called zaghrouta. El-Sayed paused as the room reacted. "I don't know how one follows that up," he said. El-Sayed then moved from identity and domestic policy into foreign policy and Israel. As he spoke about creating a society supportive of all, some of his backers began corralling a Fox News Digital reporter, blocking footage and repeatedly demanding that the credentialed reporter move away from the stage, where the other media was freely gathered. One of them, Omar Kurdi, a featured speaker at the summit, had just whispered in the ear of Barmada, the anti-Israel activist wearing the kefiyyeh turban. Kurdi, a singer and rehabilitation nonprofit executive from Cincinnati, Kurdi published a song, "I am Palestinian," last October, accompanied by a music video incorporating anti-Israel protest footage and repeatedly using the refrain, "From the river to the sea, liberation is all I see." Andoni arrived and questioned why Fox News Digital was reporting on a "cultural" event that wasn't "political." Finally, the foundation's co-founders intervened and told them to stop harassing the Fox News Digital reporter. JEWISH LEADERS IN MICHIGAN PREPARE TO WORK WITH ABDUL EL-SAYED DESPITE LINGERING CONCERNS At the microphone, El-Sayed invoked "self-determination" and developed an argument about America's role in the international system created after World War II. "The beauty of this country is our ideals," El-Sayed said. "We led the effort in this country to build a rules-based international order," he continued. "We built the United Nations and the World Health Organization and the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court so that we could uphold the ideals of democracy. We did that. And then we proceeded to be the chief violator of exactly those same ideals. To call our country to those ideals became an open question, how could you?" El-Sayed's attack on the "rules-based international order" echoed language used late last year by Singham, whose financial network has supported CodePink and other left-wing organizations. Singham argued that the existing order was built on a false narrative of World War II and called for a "new world order" based on multilateralism advanced by Chinese President Xi Jinping and the Communist Party of China. "The international rules-based order was created by another lie," Singham said. "If we want to therefore have a new world order that is based on the multilateralism that President Xi and CPC and China have proposed, we have to undo the ideological damage that has been done by the narrative of World War II," Singham had said. El-Sayed turned specifically to Palestinians. "I don't know why we cannot call for equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination," he said. "I don't know why can't we call for the idea that a Palestinian child should be able to grow up in the land of their forefathers without having to worry about a bomb paid for by our tax dollars dropping on them." "We don't want our tax dollars spent abroad to do genocide, apartheid, and war," El-Sayed said, repeating a talking point of protesters from the red-green alliance, like Benjamin, Barry and Barbada. "We believe in equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination." Andoni made his own priorities explicit in an interview with Fox News Digital after the speech. Asked what he wanted El-Sayed to tackle first in the Senate, the foundation chairman didn't hesitate. "Cutting aid to Israel," Andoni said. "Military aid especially." "That is from our perspective as a community probably number one," he said. Andoni acknowledged that El-Sayed himself had emphasized issues including "Medicare for all." "If it's up to me," Andoni said, cutting military aid to Israel "is what I will advise him." No mention was made of the fact that Prtesident Trump last week announced an end to the $4 billion in aid the U.S. currently provides to Israel. Andoni also embraced the presidential speculation. "I would love for that," he told Fox News Digital, before questioning whether America was ready for an El-Sayed presidency. ‘TROJAN HORSES’ IN AMERICA: CONGRESS PROBES INFLUENCE NETWORKS TIED TO CHINA, IRAN AND CUBA The CAIR presence offered another window into the political infrastructure around El-Sayed. Abualrub's table was filled with pocket-sized trifold guides explaining what to do if "Law Enforcement Approaches You." The first tip: "You have the right to remain silent." CAIR itself is a 501(c)(3) and does not endorse political candidates, a distinction Abualrub emphasized to Fox News Digital. But CAIR's separate political advocacy arm, CAIR Action, endorsed El-Sayed, while its affiliated Unity and Justice Fund super PAC independently spent more than $445,000 supporting his Senate candidacy, according to federal campaign-finance records. A Fox News Digital review separately found more than $100,000 in contributions to El-Sayed from current or former CAIR employees or leaders. Asked what aligned CAIR with El-Sayed's message, Abualrub said the organization wanted "more aid for the Palestinians." Speaking personally, he added that he wanted "an end to the genocide and our tax dollars going to funding the genocide." But not everyone at the summit viewed El-Sayed primarily through foreign policy. Will Langhorne, a Washington resident and former professional race car driver, said there was "a lot of excitement" around El-Sayed but called presidential speculation premature. Langhorne said El-Sayed's message was about "inclusiveness and his care for Michigan and Michiganders" and issues such as health care and affordability. "A lot of people want to point to foreign policy issues," Langhorne said, "but that's not really what was important to him and his message in connecting with the state of Michigan." Mohammed Al-Bidawi, an Egyptian American attendee, saw something different in the presidential speculation: representation. "It's interesting to see someone, his name is Abd al-Rahman, and people ask him to run for president in United States," Al-Bidawi told Fox News Digital. Even if El-Sayed never succeeded in such a campaign, he said, a Muslim and Arab American running for president would demonstrate that "we are equal." Another attendee, Hisham, who said he was from Palestine, urged patience. "I think he should focus on being a senator for now," he said. "Let him prove himself as a senator. And then he can go for a bigger" office. The political rhetoric was repeatedly interspersed with cultural celebration. In the front row, a few seat away from Benjamin and Barmada, popular Jordanian singer Hussam Allabad stood up with a wide smile and interrupted El-Sayed, recording himself in a selfie video as he led the crowd in a traditional Jordanian ahāzīj, rhythmic Arab folk chants built around call-and-response singing and synchronized clapping, a tradition commonly performed at weddings and other celebrations. El-Sayed eventually brought his remarks back to the significance of his election and the conflict with Israel. "Michigan proved that Arab America is America, too," he said. "We want an America where we stand with democracy against genocide," El-Sayed continued. "We want an America where we uphold international law." "We want an America where our tax dollars are spent to invest in our fellow Americans rather than to buy bombs and tanks for other people's countries." The Arab America Foundation then honored El-Sayed with its first "Pathbreaker Award." Then, about 40 minutes after his SUV first pulled up to the Marriott, the night's themes converged in one final exchange. At 8:20 p.m., as foundation board members took their final photographs with him, a supporter handed El-Sayed a baseball cap. El-Sayed studied the words across its front and smiled widely. "JD HABIBI." The phrase from his election-night victory speech had become political merchandise. With the "JD HABIBI" cap on, El-Sayed walked off the stage and back through the side door, passing through a security chute created by volunteers to hold back the crowd. Outside at the security entrance, Fox News Digital asked asked El-Sayed why he had created Habibi PAC and whether he was seeking higher office. This time, he paused. El-Sayed stared toward the camera and pointed to the "JD HABIBI" hat. And that's, when asked if he's seeking higher office as president, he responded, "Nope, I want to serve my state as U.S. senator." Then he ducked into the waiting GMC Yukon Denali SUV. His security detail paused long enough for him to complete the thought before shutting the door. At 8:24 p.m., 45 minutes after arriving, the Yukon pulled away with El-Sayed inside. Back in the ballroom, CodePink's Benjamin danced to a live performance by Franco-Algerian singer Nadir Benmansour, weaving between dancers with her arms overhead. Former Al Jazeera bureau chief Abderrahim Foukara posted a video of Benjamin dancing. His headline captured the dual character of the evening: "Of protest and celebration." The political activism continued after the celebration ended. Saturday night, the anti-Israel activist Barmada caused a disturbance with other activists at a Washington Capitals ice hockey game, unfurling an Israeli flag smeared with red paint resembling blood and the words: "ISRAEL KILLS." She later posted a celebratory video of their antics. "Get out of here!" hockey fans yelled. And Sunday evening, Benjamin posted a carefully curated video on Instagram, headlined "A NEW DAWN IN CONGRESS" and featuring highlights from Friday night, including Barry's footage of her hands raised in triumph as El-Sayed took the stage. "There is hope," she exclaimed, over the live music from the summit's ballroom. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.title: Trump's redistricting gamble faces reckoning as GOP holdouts claim vindication
articles.summary: Republicans' mid-decade redistricting gambit in North Carolina, Florida and Texas appeared to backfire as Democrats held key seats in the blue wave.
articles.body: Under intense pressure from the White House and conservative activists, Indiana Republicans resisted an effort to redraw the state's congressional map to favor the GOP ahead of the midterms. Now, with Republicans reeling from major election losses, a state lawmaker who helped block the plan believes the opposition may have spared Indiana's GOP delegation a political wipeout. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance pushed Republican-led states to redraw congressional maps mid-decade, but the strategy failed to deliver several anticipated pickups as Democrats flipped seats previously considered safely Republican. Indiana Senate President Pro Tempore Rod Bray, R-Martinsville, who helped lead opposition to the proposed redraw, told Fox News Digital that the plan could have devastated the state's Republican congressional delegation. "[H]ad we made a change to redistricting, we'd've ended up with something like 8-1 or 7-2 [favoring Democrats] — I really do believe that," Bray said. REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES Vance personally pressed Indiana Republicans to redraw their congressional districts, visiting Indianapolis twice and meeting privately with lawmakers, including Bray. Trump also advocated for a redraw and singled out Bray while warning Republican holdouts that they could face MAGA-backed primary challengers. Fox News Digital contacted the White House and the vice president's office for comment but did not receive a response before publication. North Carolina offered a prominent example of the risks Republican mapmakers faced as Democrats won districts the GOP had expected to hold. Former North Carolina House Speaker Tim Moore, R-Kings Mountain, helped engineer the state's Republican-friendly redistricting strategy, only to lose his own congressional seat to Democratic political newcomer LaKesha Womack. Moore did not respond to a request for comment. National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C., who led House Republicans' campaign arm, also lost his Fort Bragg-area seat to former West Virginia state Sen. Richard Ojeda. Democratic Rep. Don Davis, meanwhile, survived despite the addition of Republican-leaning areas such as Emerald Isle and Down East to his district. Western Carolina University political scientist Chris Cooper warned before the election that North Carolina Republicans risked spreading their voters too thin. "They can't spread too much thinner, or else they'll be at risk of what folks call a dummymander, where you end up hurting yourself," Cooper told Axios in April. In Florida, Democratic Reps. Jared Moskowitz and Lois Frankel, whose district includes Mar-a-Lago, survived despite redistricting efforts intended to improve Republican prospects. Democrat Pia Dandiya also won a redrawn district near Lake Okeechobee considered a "Trump +10" seat. In Texas, Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez also survived in districts along the U.S.-Mexico border that Republicans had sought to make more favorable to their candidates. Those results suggest that Republican redistricting failed to produce several anticipated pickups. Whether the strategy actually cost the party seats, however, remains a separate question from whether a broader Democratic wave overwhelmed districts that had become more Republican on paper. "Given how the newly proposed maps would have added even more Democratic voters in seemingly safe Republican districts, it is possible the redistricting, had it gone through, would backfire and actually would have given Democrats more seats," University of Indianapolis political scientist Laura Merrifield Wilson told Fox News Digital. Wilson noted that Democrats flipped only one of Indiana's nine congressional districts. "As it was, they did flip (Rep. Victoria Spartz') IN-5 from red to blue and that was a district that was considered 'solid Republican' at the beginning of this election cycle," Wilson said. "Adding more Democratic voters to those Republican districts could have actually tipped the scales in favor of the Democratic candidates." Bray explained why he believed the rejected map would have put more Republican seats at risk. "If you take the Democrat strongholds in the state of Indiana that are Marion County and obviously Northwest Indiana, and then you spread those out amongst all the congressional districts among the state, by definition you're going to weaken these other congressional districts," Bray said. He added that redrawing district boundaries would also force Republican incumbents to campaign in unfamiliar territory, potentially weakening their existing fundraising and constituent networks. Resisting the White House came with political consequences for Indiana Republicans. Wilson noted that most Republican state senators who opposed the redraw and subsequently faced primary challenges lost their races, with Sens. Greg Goode, R-Terre Haute, and Spencer Deery, R-West Lafayette, among the exceptions. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "The redistricting debacle proved to be a waste of time, energy, and money," she told Fox News Digital. Bray said he believed resisting the redraw was worthwhile. "There was an immense amount of political capital spent on both sides of this darn thing," Bray said. "It was not a good idea to start, at least from my perspective." "Indiana didn't want it," he added. "I think the results would have been far worse had we done it. So it was worthwhile. Yes." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The election leaves Republicans confronting two possible explanations: Their aggressive redistricting may have spread GOP voters too thin, exposing previously safe seats, or the Democratic wave may simply have been too powerful for even Republican-friendly maps to withstand. For Indiana Republicans who resisted Trump's demands, the results offer a measure of vindication, though the consequences of adopting the rejected map remain uncertain. "You can get far too cute with redistricting if you want to, and some folks think that they have the means or the science to just draw maps and come up with a result that they can guarantee," Bray said. "That is not the case." "We continue to hold elections for a reason. Because sometimes the results are not exactly what we expect."

articles.title: Democrats push to restore Afghanistan TPS as Trump mulls deportation flights
articles.summary: Advocates are hopeful they’ll be able to head off scheduled flights to deport Afghan nationals by forcing a vote on a bill to reinstate protections that were scrapped under President Trump. Rep. Jason Crow (R-Colo.), a veteran who was deployed to Afghanistan, will file a discharge petition Monday night to force a vote on a…
articles.body:
Advocates are hopeful they’ll be able to head off scheduled flights to deport Afghan nationals by forcing a vote on a bill to reinstate protections that were scrapped under President Trump.

Rep. Jason Crow (R-Colo.), a veteran who was deployed to Afghanistan, will file a discharge petition Monday night to force a vote on a bill that would preserve Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Afghans.

The effort comes as the administration has threatened to deport Afghan nationals to Pakistan as soon as mid-November as part of a plan to then return them to their home country of Afghanistan.

“Our Afghan partners put their lives on the line to help protect American servicemembers like me. After more than two decades of war, we made a promise that we’d look after them. It’s both a moral and national security imperative that we keep that promise,” Crow said in a statement.

“I’m working to force a vote that will protect Afghans already in the United States because I won’t let our nation leave these brave Afghans behind.”

Slightly over 8,000 Afghans risk deportation back to the country after the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) ended TPS for Afghanistan. The Supreme Court over the summer found the courts had little power to review the suspensions of TPS, allowing the protections to be stripped for citizens of 13 different countries.

Afghans are in a unique position among former TPS holders. Many came to the U.S. during the chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan and some have had trouble securing other statuses, either struggling to make it through the asylum backlog or who encourtering difficulties in meeting the numerous requirements to secure the Special Immigrant Visa given to those who served alongside U.S. military members.

Deporting these Afghans threatens to deliver U.S. allies into a situation where they could face retribution by the Taliban. The group in immigration custody facing deportation includes women.

Court battles to block the deportations have had some initial success, but in one court filing, DHS nonetheless said they plan to continue with deportation flights scheduled for Nov. 16.

The plan is facing other roadblocks as well. Pakistan has said the plan is still under review. Meanwhile, the Taliban has said they are opposed.

“The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan expresses its serious concern over reports that the United States intends to deport some Afghan refugees to Pakistan who have not yet been able to obtain legal residency documents in that country,” foreign ministry spokesperson Abdul Qahar Balkhi said in a statement to EuroNews .

Shawn VanDiver, president of #AfghanEvac, called their opposition significant.

“When even the Taliban say they have ‘serious concern’ about your deportation plan, it is time to stop and ask what you are doing,” he said in a statement.

“Pakistan and the Taliban are at each other’s throats, the border between them is nearly shut, and this administration wants to drop the families of America’s allies in the middle of it. That is not immigration enforcement. It is abandonment with a boarding pass. These families stood with our troops. Stop the flight.”

Publicly, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has not commented on deportation plans.

“ICE does not comment on prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations, or individual case details,” the agency said in a statement.

“For operational security reasons and the safety of our officers, we would not confirm future removal operations.”

But moving ahead with the TPS bill is no small task either.

Crow has bipartisan support. Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) and Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) who released a campaign video asserting that Trump had gone too far on immigration – are among the measure’s co-sponsors.

Crow will also have to net 218 signatures, winning over four GOP members, in order to force a vote on the floor.

Such a move is not unprecedented in the House. Earlier this year, the chamber passed a bill to restore TPS for Haiti when several GOP members backed a discharge petition to restore protections for citizens of that country.

But the bill has languished in the Senate, where GOP leadership has not brought it to the floor.

The same fate could easily face an Afghan TPS bill, as Senate Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) has been a vocal opponent of past efforts to give status to Afghans who entered the country as part of the evacuation effort under the Biden administration.

Waiting until Democrats retake both chambers next year comes with its own set of complications.

A bill must have been introduced for a certain amount of time before it is considered ripe for a discharge petition and it also remains unclear whether and when the Trump administration might move ahead with the flights.

“This is about America keeping our word. Thousands of Afghans risked their lives alongside American troops because our country made them a promise: We would not abandon them. Now, we risk sending them back into the hands of the very Taliban forces they helped us fight,” Rep. Sam Liccardo (D-Calif.), a co-sponsor of the measure with Crow, said in a statement.

“This cannot wait until the Democratic majority takes over—we need to reinstate Temporary Protected Status immediately and keep our friends safe.”

images.caption: Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.) arrives to the House Chamber for a series of votes on Tuesday, September 1, 2026.

articles.title: Democrats must not cede power via permitting bill that would fast-track data centers
articles.summary: A new opinion piece criticizes the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, arguing that it facilitates the rapid expansion of hyper-scale data centers and gas power plants while limiting community opposition and future regulatory oversight.
articles.body:
Here we go again. Remember the dirty deal, when the Inflation Reduction Act was held hostage by Sen. Joe Manchin (D-W.Va.) unless Congress agreed to approve the Mountain Valley Pipeline against the wishes of landowners and tribal members along the route in West Virginia and Virginia?

Everyone recognizes the need to speed up permitting and construction of cheap and clean energy, so that families aren’t stuck with rising electricity bills for the rest of their lives. But the fossil fuel industry, which is already raking in obscene windfall profits from the Iran war, wants its pound of flesh. Make that tons of flesh.

Because along with transmission lines, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 is industry’s chance to shove hyper-scale data centers down the throats of communities that are suspicious of them or outright don’t want them.

Although touted as a bill to streamline long-distance transmission lines, it would actually prevent future administrations from cleaning up the grid. Here’s how our friends at Oil Change International put it : “This bill will make it virtually impossible for communities and individuals to challenge infrastructure projects that threaten their air and water. It comes as communities across the U.S. face an unprecedented buildout of gas power plants currently being planned to fuel the AI data center boom. If the current slate of data centers and associated gas power plants move ahead, the power sector’s gas consumption could rise by 50 percent, the equivalent of the gas consumption of Central and South America combined. This would be disastrous for our climate and the communities whose air and water would be poisoned.”

And the Denver-based conservation advocacy group Center For Western Priorities’ analysis states : “The bill would give President Trump and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum two years to approve data centers on public lands. Then, in the name of certainty it would make those approvals nearly impossible for a future president to undo even if the permits were granted illegally. It also makes taxpayers pay developers if a future administration slows down a whole category of projects.”

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would lock in decisions made now, even if better alternatives become available. It naively relies on the good faith implementation by the White House and federal agencies, which have already demonstrated a disregard for the law, an irrational aversion to wind and solar, and an unhealthy obsession with fossil fuel dominance. It would allow the federal government to override objections by communities and states when they have concerns about negative impacts about projects.

Even the most optimistic model forecasts an increase in harmful greenhouse gas emissions with the passage of Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. Proponents rationalize the bill by saying that emissions will rise even more without it. This is playing to “lose by less.” We can do much better by waiting until clean energy proponents are more powerful in Congress and in the executive branch.

Co-sponsor Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) is understandably flummoxed, perhaps infuriated, by the federal government’s rescinding of off-shore wind permits, and is trying to ensure that can’t happen again. But the timing of this bill is bizarre. In just two months, wind energy supporters will be in a much more powerful position in both chambers, with the opportunity to negotiate a better bill. Why are they planning to ram it through during the lame duck Congress, when they are at their weakest?

In future campaigns for office, today’s senators and Congress members from both parties are going to have to explain why they voted to fast track hyper-scale data centers. They can avoid all that squirming by killing the bill now.

Kenny Bruno is a senior advisor to Bold Alliance , and a longtime pipeline fighter and campaigner for environmental health.

images.caption: An aerial view shows an Amazon data center under construction in New Florence, Mo., Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/Jeff Roberson)

articles.title: Burgum’s security blocks TMZ reporter: ‘You’re banging into me’
articles.summary: A TMZ reporter got into a confrontation with security for Interior Secretary Doug Burgum at Washington Reagan National Airport. In the beginning of a video posted to the social platform X on Monday, TMZ’s Charlie Cotton appears to be holding the camera and standing next to Burgum at the airport when he says, “I’m with…
articles.body:
A TMZ reporter got into a confrontation with security for Interior Secretary Doug Burgum at Washington Reagan National Airport.

In the beginning of a video posted to the social platform X on Monday, TMZ’s Charlie Cotton appears to be holding the camera and standing next to Burgum at the airport when he says, “I’m with TMZ. Can I just ask you just one question, sir?”

The video then shows Burgum shaking his head in response to Cotton as he looks down at his phone. Cotton presses again for a question, and Burgum starts to walk away. As Cotton continues pressing, a man on security detail for Burgum steps in between Cotton and Burgum, and Cotton is heard saying, “Please don’t touch me, sir.”

The security guard for Burgum then says he is “not touching” Cotton, to which Cotton replies that he is “banging into me.”

Cotton continues to try to follow Burgum, with the guard in front of him.

“Doug, I’ve just got a simple question. Usually a president in Trump’s position, being a lame duck would be ineffective, do you think that’s going to be true of President Trump?” Cotton asks as he continues to follow Burgum, with the secretary not responding.

As the guard, Burgum and Cotton exit the airport, Cotton then alleges the guard has “been touching me far too many times,” with the guard getting right in front of him again.

“I’m not impeding his process,” Cotton protests. “I’m not a threat at all, so you can’t touch me like that. That’s unbelievable. I was not a threat.”

Burgum then gets into a car, and the guard closes the door.

In a statement emailed to The Hill on Monday, a spokesperson for the Department of the Interior said that Burgum’s “security detail takes their mission seriously and conducts themselves professionally 24/7, 365. Full stop.”

“The video clearly shows the detail’s actions followed protocol. We thank his security detail for their service and dedication every single day.”

articles.title: Trump tells DHS chief to work with Democrats on immigration reform, but no amnesty
articles.summary: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says Trump told him to engage Democrats on immigration reform but insists amnesty will never happen.
articles.body: President Donald Trump has encouraged Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to work with Democrats who have reached out about immigration reform, but the administration has not discussed changing its enforcement policies and remains opposed to amnesty, Mullin reportedly said Monday. Mullin told reporters on the sidelines of a counter-drone conference in Maryland that "a lot of Democrats" have contacted him about working together on immigration legislation in the new Congress. "I’ve let the president know that those calls are coming in, and the president has said, ‘Let’s start working with them and then let’s meet at some point,’" Mullin said. WHITE HOUSE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER TRUMP ANGERS BASE BY FLOATING ILLEGAL ALIEN DEAL WITH DEMS However, Mullin emphasized that he and Trump have not discussed changing the administration’s immigration enforcement policies. "But has there been a conversation about changing the policy?" Mullin said of his discussions with Trump. "No, we haven’t had that conversation." "We’re never going to allow amnesty to happen," Mullin added. Mullin also suggested Congress could consider a pathway to permanent legal status for recipients of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, which provides temporary protection from deportation and work authorization to eligible immigrants brought to the country illegally as children. HOUSE GOP ERUPTS AT STEPHEN MILLER AS TRUMP ELEVATES HIM AFTER MIDTERM MASSACRE: 'MEGALOMANIAC' "If we want to have an immigration reform to where we can look at DACA and figure out a way that these individuals can become maybe legal permanent citizens or something like this, that’ll be up to Congress," Mullin said. Mullin’s comments come after Trump signaled openness to working with Democrats on immigration following the 2026 midterm elections , even as the president named Stephen Miller , the architect of his administration’s hardline immigration policies, as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Mullin’s willingness to consider a legislative pathway for DACA recipients marks a shift in tone from the department’s messaging earlier this year. In a March post on X, DHS stressed that DACA "does not confer any form of legal status in this country" and warned that recipients could be arrested and deported, including for criminal conduct. The post also included video of Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., questioning then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem. Durbin asked whether Noem was aware that DACA immigrants must undergo criminal background checks. Noem responded that the agency follows the law in its detention and deportation decisions. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER DHS said in the post that ICE arrested 264 DACA recipients nationwide between Jan. 20 and Sept. 28, 2025, and that more than 92% had been charged with or convicted of a crime in the United States. Mullin’s comments Monday marked his first public suggestion that DACA recipients could gain permanent legal status through congressional action. DHS did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment by publication time.

articles.title: Erika Kirk blasts ‘beyond disgusting’ jokes after Dave Chappelle mocks Charlie Kirk’s assassination
articles.summary: “Ever since that guy Charlie Kirk got murdered, and I shouldn’t say this publicly, but I feel better,” Chappelle told fans at Madison Square Garden on Saturd...
articles.body:
Hours after Dave Chappelle made light of right-wing provocateur Charlie Kirk's slaying, Kirk's widow lashed out Sunday at "podcasters, comedians, and commentators" laughing "about political assassination."

Erika Kirk, CEO of the youth-focused conservative group Turning Point USA, said that such humor is "beyond disgusting" and that she fears for the "moral decay" of America.

"To see leftist podcasters, comedians, and commentators laugh about political assassination as though it's entertainment and the destruction of a human life is a punchline, is beyond disgusting," she said on X .

"My husband, Charlie Kirk, was killed in an act of political violence, something our two children and I will live with every day for the rest of our lives," she said. "A culture that laughs at assassination is one of profound moral decay."

While Kirk didn't mention Chappelle by name, her comments came after his gig Saturday night at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

"Ever since that guy Charlie Kirk got murdered, and I shouldn't say this publicly, but I feel better," Chappelle said, according to fan videos of the show circulating online, which drew a smattering of uncomfortable chuckles from the stunned room.

In another clip from Madison Square Garden that was making the rounds, Chappelle said, "I'm sure Charlie Kirk is looking up at us right now, laughing so hard he can't breathe."

Erika Kirk's denunciation also comes in the wake of an apology from the hosts of the "I've Had It" podcast for making light of the assassination.

"On Thursday's show, we laughed at a joke about Charlie Kirk," Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan said in a joint statement Saturday. "It was an insensitive joke, and we should not have laughed. We regret it, and we apologize."

Welch and Sullivan were reading social media posts about the midterm elections and laughed at one that read, "We're digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again."

Charlie Kirk, 31, was gunned down on Sept. 10 last year during an outdoor speaking appearance at Utah Valley University. Former UVU student Tyler Robinson is accused of the slaying .

"You do not have to agree with someone's politics to recognize the value of their life," Erika Kirk said Sunday. "This should not be so hard. Political violence must never be something this country tolerates, excuses, or celebrates."

Before the Kirk comment, some conservatives had embraced Chappelle for his years of mocking the transgender community .

That goodwill has most likely come to an end.

"Chappelle is just not funny anymore," conservative megadonor Elon Musk said Sunday night on X . Reacting to one of the Madison Square Garden clips, Musk wrote, " Dave Chappelle is cruel ."

A representative for Chappelle did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to build border barrier in Big Bend National Park despite bipartisan backlash
articles.summary: "We are killing a gnat with a sledgehammer and wasting a colossal amount of money," said Texas Judge Greg Henington, a Republican.
articles.body:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to bypass regulations and build a border barrier in Texas's scenic Big Bend National park — a project that has been paused several times in recent months amid lawsuits and opposition on both the left and the right.

In an unsigned opinion, the court said that Congress had expressed a "clear preference for expeditious border construction," which outweighs "any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm."

Previously, a federal judge had halted the project , allowing litigation to proceed without further loss of protected wilderness and questioning whether Big Bend National Park meets Congress's fast-track definition of an area with "high illegal entry." The Supreme Court effectively dismissed those arguments.

In August, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Commissioner Rodney Scott announced that he was temporarily "pausing all construction activity" in Big Bend.

"Last night I put a pause on all activity in that park as far as construction goes until I can get down there and do a personal evaluation," Scott said in a video posted to social media , adding that he would "talk to some stakeholders, talk to some local law enforcement in that area" to "ensure that we secure our borders while simultaneously protecting BBNP for generations to come."

Earlier that month, government contractors started bulldozing sensitive areas of Big Bend as part of the Trump administration's $46.5 billion push to expand border barriers along the U.S.-Mexico border — a move that triggered fierce bipartisan backlash.

"I believe in border security 100%," Terrell County Sheriff Thaddeus Cleveland, a Republican and former Border Patrol agent, told Fox San Antonio . "Believe in even installation of barriers where they're needed. But I can tell you that specific area ... even just what they've done, unnecessary."

Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas also sent a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin relaying his constituents' concerns.

"My constituents believe that the 1,000-foot riverbank cliffs and remote Big Bend terrain offers its own source of deterrence for any illegal migrants crossing into the United States," Cornyn wrote. "Many residents that live and work around the parks are also concerned that a physical wall, which would be accompanied by lighting systems, access roads, and maintenance corridors, would (1) ruin the beauty, landscape, and wildlife of the park, (2) threaten culturally significant Native American sites, (3) disrupt wildlife migration, (4) limit access to the Rio Grande River, and (5) significantly harm the local economy as tourism is a major economic driver for the region."

Since returning to office in January 2025, President Trump has taken action to remove protections from more than 86 million acres of public lands, according to a recent analysis by the Center for American Progress (CAP), a liberal think tank.

Here's everything you need to know about what's happening in Big Bend — and how it connects to Trump's broader agenda.

Established in 1944, Big Bend encompasses more than 800,000 acres of scorching Chihuahuan desert, cool, craggy peaks and fertile Rio Grande valley. It's located in a remote pocket of the Lone Star State formed by a huge southward dip in the river, and it contains within its boundaries 517 miles of U.S.-Mexico border. The park's diverse landscape is home to 56 species of reptiles, 75 species of mammals, more than 450 species of birds and more than 1,200 species of plants. Sea fossils, dinosaur bones and volcanic dikes have also been found there.

The National Park Service describes Big Bend as a "hiker's paradise," with more than 150 miles of desert and mountain trails — including the 1,500-foot vertical limestone walls of Santa Elena Canyon and Lost Mine's sweeping valley views. Designated a Gold Tier International Dark Sky Park in 2012, Big Bend is one of the best places in the U.S. to see the Milky Way at night.

"Easily top 10 park for me," one Reddit commenter wrote . "Borderline top 5."

"It's so far out there — really remote — which helps make it feel more magical," another added.

Is Trump really building a border wall in Big Bend?

Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill — which passed in July 2025 over unanimous Democratic opposition — included $46.5 billion in funding for hundreds of miles of new border barriers, and early CBP maps showed "a bold line of wall structure along the floodplain of most of the Rio Grande in the high desert region of Far West Texas," according to the Washington Post .

But after residents and local officials objected, the administration quietly altered its plans, nixing its usual 30-foot steel bollard fence in favor of 17 miles of "vehicle barriers" — interconnected steel X's, 4 to 6 feet in height — along with surveillance cameras, lights, sensors and a new patrol road that will run the length of the park, at a cost of $1.7 billion.

In August, bulldozers belonging to Southwest Valley Constructors started work on the patrol road. According to the Post , " images show vehicle treads left behind on the dusty terrain as animals such as hoofed javelinas wander past. Construction crews were spotted surveying the land and marking the road's planned route."

"Early construction activities such as clearing and grubbing have begun," a CBP spokesman confirmed in a statement to the outlet.

At the time, CBP denied that its contractors would have to dynamite the mountainside to complete the road — but advocates insisted that "if they're going to build on that [rock], there is no alternative to blasting," as Bob Krumenaker, former Big Bend superintendent for the National Park Service, told the Post. Krumenaker predicted that blasting would alter the view, disturb nesting falcons and send debris spilling into the Rio Grande.

In August, the Daily Mail reported that "demolition crews have already begun blowing craters into the bedrock" with "sticks of TNT" just outside the park.

"'They've been blowing things up for about the last two weeks," one border agent told the paper. "Underneath the surface is rock, not dirt. They have to blow it up in order to build the wall. No one knows about it because there's no one out here to see it, but the project is moving ahead."

In response, a CBP spokesman told the Daily Mail that "construction crews are onsite re-grading roads that were damaged by recent storms that are required for access to conduct surveys."

Wait, how can the administration build anything in a national park?

In order to speed construction of the border wall — which slowed to a crawl during Trump's first term amid lawsuits and property ownership disputes — the Department of Homeland Security has waived its contractors from complying with dozens of laws, including the Endangered Species Act and the National Environmental Policy Act. This means CBP can disregard the project's impact on certain plants and animals while skipping lengthy reviews and avoiding public input. According to the Center for Biological Diversity , "the move marks the first time in American history that the federal government has cast aside a broad slate of environmental laws … in a national park."

In his letter, Cornyn complained about the administration's lack of "coordination and communication" with "Texas stakeholders," saying it "has not been as fulsome as in prior years."

"On April 16, fourteen Texas-Mexico Border County Judges wrote to you asking for DHS to engage with the communities they serve and have open communication about the upcoming installation of border security measures," Cornyn wrote. "To my knowledge, the county judges have not received a response to their April 16 letter."

The administration's approach to Big Bend is part of a larger pattern.

In March 2025, Trump signed an executive order designed to expand logging and reduce oversight across about 250 million acres of national forests and protected public lands — a move that could damage fragile ecosystems, threaten old-growth forests, increase pollution and even worsen wildfires, according to environmentalists.

In April, a border wall contractor partially bulldozed — or "inadvertently disturbed," as CBP later put it — a giant, ancient Native American etching in the floor of the Arizona desert.

In July, the president signed proclamations to shrink two major national monuments in southern Utah — Bears Ears National Monument and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument — by roughly 91% in order to open previously protected land to uranium and coal mining. Similar rollbacks have also occurred in Alaska, where the administration has opened new sites to oil drilling.

All told, the Trump administration has "cumulatively removed or initiated removal of protections for more than 100 million acres of public lands across both terms," according to CAP — more than one-third of the amount of land that President Theodore Roosevelt initially protected during his time in office.

According to the Post, Big Bend "community members have sued the federal government in court, filed complaints with environmental protection agencies, opposed permits for contractors seeking use of local roads and wells, and demanded accountability in public meetings."

Protesters gathered at the park in August to voice their opposition , and public officials from both parties have called the administration's project disruptive and redundant, noting that " near zero " crossings occur within the park itself.

"God already built a wall through Big Bend — it's called the Chisos Mountains," then-Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico wrote on X . "We don't need to give billions of our tax dollars to out of state vendors. We don't need to desecrate this sacred land. We don't need this useless, disgraceful, corrupt Big Bend border wall."

"The potential destruction from road construction over the rugged terrain of Mariscal Mountain is extreme," Texas Rep. Lloyd Doggett, also a Democrat, said in a July 31 news release . "Tons of rock blasted away could end up impacting Mariscal Canyon, the Rio Grande, and Mexico. An incredible waste of both taxpayer money and an invaluable place of spectacular beauty!"

"Major permanent infrastructure, accompanied by lighting systems, access roads, and maintenance corridors would permanently alter one of the most remote and ecologically significant border landscapes in the United States," five border sheriffs, including Cleveland, wrote in a March statement . "Border security is not a one-size-fits-all proposition. Strategies that may be appropriate in high-traffic urban sectors are not necessarily appropriate in geographically remote regions such as ours."

"We are killing a gnat with a sledgehammer and wasting a colossal amount of money," Brewster County, Texas, Judge Greg Henington said at the time . Henington is a Republican.

In August, U.S. House candidate Brandon Herrera — a Republican running to represent the Big Bend area in Congress — said in a statement that he opposes "any construction in the Big Bend area that disturbs the natural landscape and threatens the jobs that tourism brings where non-intrusive technology would do the job."

GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledged in July that the administration should "take into account the local community's concerns." But he also argued that Trump's "border wall" won't always look like a literal wall.

"When we say build a wall, in some respects, it's a metaphor," Johnson told reporters. "It means we have to have a border that is secure."

articles.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
articles.summary: Jensen Huang is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
articles.body:
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.

Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.

In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.

The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.

"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.

Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.

It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.

The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.

But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.

For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.

"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.

It think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.

Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy

The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.

We don't know when their affair began or ended , but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.

China denies that she was engaged in espionage.

Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.

China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.

Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.

Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.

He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.

Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.

At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.

Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.

An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.

And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.

Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.

He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.

While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.

And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

articles.title: Sullivan campaign files motion against Peltola over rejected absentee ballot lawsuit
articles.summary: Sen. Dan Sullivan’s (R-Alaska) campaign on Monday filed a motion against Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign to intervene in its rejected absentee ballot lawsuit. Her campaign sued the state of Alaska on Friday to obtain access to records for absentee ballots that were rejected by the Alaska Division of Elections. “It should surprise no…
articles.body:
Sen. Dan Sullivan’s (R-Alaska) campaign on Monday filed a motion against Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign to intervene in its rejected absentee ballot lawsuit.

Her campaign sued the state of Alaska on Friday to obtain access to records for absentee ballots that were rejected by the Alaska Division of Elections.

“It should surprise no one that the same D.C. lawyers who spent more than a year conspiring with Mary Peltola’s campaign to deceive Alaskan voters are now asking a court to let her campaign ignore Alaska law and change the rules while votes are still being counted,” Sullivan campaign spokesperson Nate Adams, said in a statement.

Adams accused Peltola’s lawsuit of being “further evidence that she is not confident she can win on the merits alone,” further accusing the campaign of “once again attempting to rig the system in her favor.” He added that the campaign is confident that after all ballots have been counted, Dan Sullivan “will win.”

Peltola leads Dan Sullivan by more than 600 votes as of 4:55 p.m. EST last Wednesday with 30 percent of the vote still outstanding, according to The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ . She leads with 48.17 percent of the vote to his 47.88 percent.

Alaska’s vote count is expected to continue for several more days as state election officials transport ballots across large swaths of terrain. Ballots can arrive up to 15 days after the election so long as they are postmarked by Election Day.

Peltola’s campaign previously said it requested records of the rejected ballots on multiple occasions but were denied access.

The Alaska Senate race has already been the subject of litigation after the Trump administration sued to block certification of the election if Sullivan lost and argued that the presence of a candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan could confuse voters.

Federal authorities are investigating whether her campaign’s alleged recruitment of Daniel J. Sullivan was a violation of the law.

President Trump suggested in the days ahead of the election that Peltola should have been removed from the ballot and claimed that the alleged scheme was “voter fraud at the highest level” after the New York Times reported that her campaign and national Democrats worked together to recruit candidates to pull votes away from Dan Sullivan.

Peltola, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Daniel J. Sullivan have all denied any involvement in the reported effort to recruit spoiler candidates for the race.

articles.title: REBECCA GRANT: Jensen Huang owes America an apology, and Nvidia owes investors answers
articles.summary: Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese business executive suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being a recruit for espionage.
articles.body: The espionage "honeytrap" is the oldest spy trick in the book. How embarrassing that the brilliant Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, apparently fell for this Hollywood movie cliché. Huang has been a front-line warrior in America’s race to stay ahead of China in AI. How the heck did he slip up? Huang has admitted to having an affair with an unrelated Chinese business executive, Alice Huang. Huang has apologized to his family and employees. Nvidia is investigating. According to the Financial Times, Alice Huang boasted to investors about her ability to secure Nvidia chips, likely on the black market, for use in non-American data center projects in Southeast Asia. Huang’s former company, Megaspeed, is being investigated for allegedly smuggling Nvidia "chips" called GPUs. NVIDIA CASE HIGHLIGHTS RISKS OF ALLEGED 'HONEYPOT' SCHEMES TARGETING EXECUTIVES "You deserve better from me," Huang said to Nvidia employees and shareholders in a press release on Sunday. No kidding. Frankly, Huang owes America an apology. Here’s why. A Chinese assault on Nvidia is scary for Americans because Nvidia holds as much as an 80% market share of the world’s most advanced data center AI chips. Nvidia is the "go-to choice for all the biggest AI software developers," as explained by Yahoo Finance. The carelessness is unfathomable. Can you imagine if the CEO of a top U.S. defense company was caught in a close relationship with a suspected Chinese operative? One has to wonder: Does Huang not realize that Nvidia has made him a major national security player and, therefore, a target for espionage? FORMER CIA AGENT JOHN KIRIAKOU REVEALS HOW SEX PLAYS A MAJOR ROLE IN ESPIONAGE AND SPYING The U.S. intelligence community certainly had its eyes on Nvidia’s CEO. As reported by The New York Times, it turns out U.S. intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang was a Chinese recruit. The Times also reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio alerted other officials months ago to the possible shenanigans. Jensen Huang has been a star. He embodies the American dream at hyperscale. He married his college sweetheart, his daughter, son and son-in-law all work in the family business, and he’s become a titan on the level of Henry Ford. Remember when Huang flew on Air Force One with President Trump to Beijing back in May? We were all so proud of him. AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD Winning the race with China – whether in the Pacific, in space or in AI – is the top challenge for America, as laid out by all the recent national security strategies from both the Biden administration and Trump’s White House. Aside from the nuclear triad, the AI race may be the single most important contest shaping the world today. AI is as important as the submarine fleet and space superiority. NVIDIA SHARES FALL AFTER INVESTIGATION INTO CEO'S RELATIONSHIP WITH ALLEGED CHINESE SPY To win the AI competition, the U.S. must conquer global market share. Nvidia chips won’t do it alone. The overall goal is for U.S. products to dominate the AI tech stack – chips, software, models, experts and, yes, data centers. That is why Amazon Web Services, for example, has a global network in 39 regions and why you see Google investing $15 billion in Malaysia, alongside $17 billion in Wyoming. Maintaining the lead requires a robust base of global operations and sales that generate the revenue to fuel innovation. This is why Chinese companies were trying to get advanced chips. This is also why, ironically, the U.S. Department of Commerce may now permit case-by-case sales of slower H200 chips to certain Chinese companies. American tech can’t lock itself down inside the USA and give China free rein to build out data centers around the globe to undercut prices for AI services and capture global markets. Whatever happened, it looks like conduct unbecoming of an industry leader. articles.title: Jeffries vows Democrats won’t ‘give a dime’ to Trump’s deportation efforts
articles.summary: Hakeem Jeffries outlined House Democrats’ priorities after their midterm wins, vowing to oppose deportation funding and backing Pete Hegseth’s impeachment.
articles.body: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries on Monday laid out an aggressive agenda for House Democrats as the party prepares to take control of the chamber following sweeping midterm election victories, declaring that Democrats will "not give a dime" toward funding the Trump administration's deportation efforts. The House minority leader made the remarks during a press conference, one week before Democrats are set to vote on whether Jeffries should remain in his leadership position. "The American people clearly and decisively rejected MAGA extremism on Tuesday and voted for dramatic change," Jeffries said. "House Democrats have taken the position that we're not going to give a dime to the administration's violent mass deportation machine," he added. DEMS PIVOT FROM ‘AFFORDABILITY’ PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS Jeffries also criticized the use of taxpayer dollars to support what he called "un-American" policies under President Donald Trump. "Taxpayer dollars should be used to make life more affordable for the American people, not brutalize or kill American citizens, and violently target law-abiding immigrant communities and families, which is what has happened over the last two years," Jeffries said. TRUMP TELLS DHS CHIEF TO WORK WITH DEMOCRATS ON IMMIGRATION REFORM, BUT NO AMNESTY He added that he hopes to secure one additional signature on a discharge petition that would bypass House leadership and force a floor vote on the American Dream and Promise Act, which would provide permanent legal status and a pathway to citizenship for Dreamers and recipients of Temporary Protected Status (TPS). "Hopefully some of our colleagues on the other side of the aisle will be willing to do that work, perhaps beginning with one additional signature that we need to force a vote on the Dream and Promise Act from a Republican," he said. Among other priorities, Jeffries said Democrats want to pass legislation banning members of the House and Senate from trading stocks, an effort aimed at restoring public trust in government. He also voiced support for an impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of the war in Iran and alleged constitutional violations. "I'm a hard yes, as I've made clear, on the impeachment resolution. Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America's national security, and he's the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed gas prices on everyday Americans, made the country less safe," Jeffries said. "Iran is stronger now than they were before," he argued. Jeffries said he plans to speak with every member of the caucus in an effort to retain his position. "I'm going to work hard to talk to every single member about what we've been able to do together over the last two years, and what the opportunities are for us to do together in the next two years," he said.

articles.title: House GOP chair calls to delay leadership elections, reform rules
articles.summary: House Ways and Means Committee Chair Jason Smith (R-Mo.) called for GOP leadership elections to be delayed, arguing that Republicans need to self-reflect on their brutal midterm losses before moving forward as a conference. “We are less than a week removed from Tuesday’s elections, and need to understand how and why we lost the trust…
articles.body:
House Ways and Means Committee Chair Jason Smith (R-Mo.) called for GOP leadership elections to be delayed, arguing that Republicans need to self-reflect on their brutal midterm losses before moving forward as a conference.

“We are less than a week removed from Tuesday’s elections, and need to understand how and why we lost the trust of the American people,” Smith wrote on X Monday.

“We also need, as a Conference, to address how our rules have empowered members to vote against rules, bills, and even the Speaker. Failing to address these issues before choosing someone new to lead our Conference is doing a disservice to whoever we choose as Republican Leader,” he added.

Republicans are slated to hold leadership elections on Tuesday. Politico had first reported that Republicans will hold a two-hour candidate forum that morning before voting on the leader, whip, conference chair and other positions.

House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) is challenging House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) for minority leader, while Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger (R-Texas) is going head-to-head against House GOP Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.). Reps. Greg Steube (R-Fla.) and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) are challenging current GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.).

Smith said in his X post that he thinks both Scalise and Jordan are “outstanding men who are more than up to the job.”

But he also noted that Republicans “should delay our Leadership elections until we decide how to hold each other accountable and what our path forward should be.”

“Our rules must never again permit a Leader to be taken hostage to the whims of an individual member. We can and must do better,” Smith wrote.
