articles.title: Gina Hinojosa Wants To Freeze Electricity Rates in Texas. New Jersey Shows Why That Won't Work.
articles.summary: In New Jersey, a rate freeze touched only part of the bill, and in some cases left ratepayers with higher bills than before.
articles.body:
When Democrat Gina Hinojosa is sworn in as Texas governor in January, one of her first acts, "within an hour of taking the oath of office," she recently told The Texas Tribune, will be to "declare a high-cost emergency in the state of Texas and issue an emergency executive order to: one, suspend the gas and diesel tax; and two, freeze electricity rates."

Hinojosa—who tied increases in property taxes and electricity bills to Republican Gov. Greg Abbott's policies— promised during her campaign that if elected, she would "direct the Public Utility Commission to freeze the rates residential customers pay until we have laws to ensure that data centers and other high-load users pay for themselves."

With Texans seeing a 3.3 percent increase in the average electricity price for residential customers between August 2025 and August 2026—roughly in line with the national increase—the state's electorate clearly found Hinojosa's pledge compelling. However, it's unclear if Hinojosa actually has the power to follow through on her campaign promise.

In Texas' decentralized market, retail providers, not regulators, set electricity prices. This means Hinojosa has very little authority over residential prices, and her order would not lower costs. But as Click2Houston.com points out, Hinojosa could still impact prices; she could use her influence over the state budget "to push lawmakers toward her priorities," including forcing data centers to pay more. Of course, this would do little to address the primary cause of nationwide electricity spikes: transmission and distribution charges.

Instead of Texas imposing price controls on the free market, Hinojosa could learn from the mistakes of New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a fellow Democrat who has failed to meaningfully lower electricity prices in her state despite signing an executive order that declared a state of emergency and froze rate hikes by the state's utilities.

Sherrill realized that even if she froze rates, it wouldn't erase the factors driving higher electricity prices, such as the supply and transmission costs providers pay. In June, to offset the increases utilities typically pass on to customers, Sherrill signed off on a budget authorization that allocates $500 million to provide ratepayers short-term relief. Yet in October, a CBS News report found that even after the rate freeze, utility costs in the Garden State remained high, with one resident remarking her electricity bill had "nearly doubled."

In July, the consulting firm E3 released a report—commissioned by Sherrill for the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities—that found that changes to state policy mainly affect distribution, which is "roughly a quarter" of the charges on residents' electricity bills, and that "no single reform or modernization option" could be presented as a standalone fix.

It's not just New Jersey that has tried (and failed) to bring down utility costs by freezing electricity rates; last July Georgia's Public Service Commission unanimously approved an agreement to freeze base power rates for at least three years. A year after the freeze was implemented, the average electricity price for residential customers in Georgia rose by 2.3 percent . Meanwhile, in October, Virginia Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger called for a six-year freeze on residential electricity rates as a condition for approving the proposed $67 billion merger between utilities Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy.

Regardless of where it's proposed, a rate freeze is a superficial fix for a problem that requires less government thumb on the scale, not more.

At least one Democratic governor has declined to use rate freezes as a temporary panacea for rising energy costs. In a March appearance on CBS 2's " The Point ," New York Gov. Kathy Hochul was asked if she thought a "two-year moratorium or freeze on utility rates statewide" was "doable." She quickly rejected the idea, favoring an "all-of-the-above approach to find more sources of energy to help drive down [costs]."

What rate freezes like Hinojosa's miss is that states have little direct impact on electric prices. As the E3 report notes , "Most of a typical bill…is set in federal and regional markets with limited ability at the state level to influence those costs."

Still, that doesn't make the idea behind these policies—that government should interfere in the market—any less harmful.

Without the price signals they receive from electricity rates, utilities can't properly plan for upgrades, expansion, or future demand. Freezing electricity rates clearly polls well as policy, but it works better on the campaign trail than in practice.

articles.title: Colom calls out election raters for writing off his Mississippi Senate campaign
articles.summary: Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom (D) blasted prominent election forecasters for underestimating his chances of defeating Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) in their election ratings, arguing that the grim predictions made it harder for Democrats to raise money and compete in the South. Colom, a Black attorney, has maintained a narrow lead over Hyde-Smith by less…
articles.body:
Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom (D) blasted prominent election forecasters for underestimating his chances of defeating Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) in their election ratings, arguing that the grim predictions made it harder for Democrats to raise money and compete in the South.

Colom, a Black attorney, has maintained a narrow lead over Hyde-Smith by less than 3,000 votes in one of the biggest surprises of last week’s midterm elections, with the race still too close to call.

In a post on social media, Colom accused the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report and other unnamed election forecasters of relying on outdated assumptions about Southern elections and overlooking candidates who could make races in deep-red states competitive.

“At some point, we have to talk about @CookPolitical and other ‘prognosticators’ who had me and other southern candidates labeled as solid R for much of the campaign cycle,” Colom wrote on the social platform X on Monday. “They made it much more difficult to fundraise and are part of the reason the South has been neglected for so long.”

The Cook Political Report had initially rated the Mississippi Senate race as “Solid Republican,” citing doubts over the ability for a Democrat to challenge Hyde-Smith in a state President Trump carried by 24 percentage points in 2024. It later shifted to “Likely Republican” in October.

Even as the race attracted more attention in the finals weeks before Election Day, forecasters remained skeptical of Colom’s chances in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

An Oct. 30 analysis from Cook Political Report described Colom’s campaign as “admirable” but noted that Republicans believed a late influx of campaign spending had helped shore up Hyde-Smith’s reelection bid.

Colom’s campaign raised $4.4 million compared to Hyde-Smith’s $6.3 million, though both parties have recently ramped up the pressure to raise more money in the surprisingly tight Senate race.

Colom said the forecasters avoid accountability when wrong about their predictions, and accused an unnamed Cook Political Report analyst of dismissing his attempts to explain why their assessment of his campaign was incorrect.

“One of their ‘analysts’ was extremely condescending to me (not Jessica) when I tried to make my pitch for why they were wrong about my rating like he knew something about MS politics when he’s never been to the Sip,” he wrote, clarifying that Senate and Governors editor Jessica Taylor was not the individual to whom he was referring.

He added that the attitude had hurt other Southern candidates in the midterms, including Louisiana Senate candidate Jamie Davis, who narrowly lost to Rep. Julia Letlow (R-La.).

The Hill has reached out to Cook Political Report for comment.

articles.title: A Capitol Hill vibe shift: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into the vibe shift on Capitol Hill with lawmakers returning to Washington for the first time since the midterm elections.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into the vibe shift on Capitol Hill with lawmakers returning to Washington for the first time since the midterm elections. Plus, Joelle Gross zeroes in on the Democratic candidates who made the furthest inroads with President Donald Trump’s voters. — Adam Wollner A blue tsunami empowers Democrats as Congress returns to Washington Analysis by Sahil Kapur The vibes are different on Capitol Hill, with Republicans still shell-shocked by the magnitude of last week’s electoral thumping as they return to Washington as lame ducks with a lengthy to-do list. Outstanding items include: Passing a government funding bill by the Dec. 11 deadline to prevent a shutdown.Passing the annual National Defense Authorization Act.Passing a farm bill for agriculture and food-assistance policy.Deciding whether — and how — to renew FISA Section 702 warrantless surveillance.Figuring out a permitting reform deal to streamline construction projects.Figuring out whether to pass or abandon a college sports bill.Reviewing President Donald Trump’s nominees in the Senate.Considering a House resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky. Democrats feel empowered by their far-reaching midterm victories, as they made deep incursions into red-leaning territory amid a voter backlash to Trump. Some say that their mandate includes ending the Iran war and that lawmakers shouldn’t pass any government funding bill without cutting off money for Trump to continue the war without congressional approval. “I believe we would abdicate our responsibility if we voted to provide billions of additional dollars for President Trump’s war of choice in Iran,” Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., a moderate, wrote in a letter to colleagues Saturday. “We must refuse to invoke cloture on any package that includes another cent for his war.” Meanwhile, a small group of Republicans is pushing to delay tomorrow’s closed-door meeting to pick their leadership team for the next two years. The top three GOP senators — John Thune of South Dakota, John Barrasso of Wyoming and Tom Cotton of Arkansas — are favored to hold their positions in the minority, but not without some pushback. “A week ago, we had the worst election result in decades. We need a discussion about what went wrong, how we fix it, what we stand for, and how our agenda must focus on the concerns of the American people,” Sen. David McCormick, R-Pa., who rarely steps out of line with GOP leadership, said in a statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward,” he added. There is no internal consensus yet among Republicans about why they lost so decisively, and many of them are reluctant to point fingers at Trump, even though the results and exit polls overwhelmingly indicate voters were delivering a rebuke of him. Thune said the election gives the GOP an “opportunity to reflect on what we as a party need to do better.” The big question for Trump and Republicans is how much they’re willing to compromise over the next six weeks, while they retain their maximum leverage, to achieve some of their year-end goals. Come Jan. 3, Democrats are poised to take power on Capitol Hill with some of the biggest majorities here since 2009. How exit poll data explains the millions of Trump voters who went blue, in maps and charts By Joelle Gross Millions of Americans who voted for President Donald Trump backed Democrats in last week’s midterm elections — that much is clear from the vote counts. But to understand why, it helps to drill down into the exit polls. Voters turned away from Trump and the Republicans out of deep frustration over the economy and concerns about the state of American democracy, an analysis of the NBC News Exit Poll data found. Democrats re-energized young and Latino voters, among other groups, fueling a historic takeover of Congress and grabbing Senate seats in states that had seemed tattooed red. Tuesday’s Democratic success came not only by mobilizing the party’s base. Senate candidates from Texas to South Carolina to New Hampshire swayed former Trump voters. In some states, percentages of Trump voters turning out for Democrats reached double digits. About 13% of voters who chose Trump in 2024 voted for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia this year, the exit poll suggests. James Talarico in Texas and Mark Warner in Virginia drew 11%. Nationally, around 7% of former Trump voters opted for Democratic candidates in House elections. By comparison, 2% of those who voted for Kamala Harris split for Republican House candidates. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Dana White takes podium at White House press briefing
articles.summary: Dana White, president and CEO of Ultimate Fighting Championship, stopped by the press briefing room Monday, participating in an impromptu press conference with President Trump. The visit comes after Trump posted a Truth Social post over the weekend offering White the press secretary position. He told reporters on Sunday that he was actually joking. White…
articles.body:
Dana White, president and CEO of Ultimate Fighting Championship, stopped by the press briefing room Monday, participating in an impromptu press conference with President Trump.

The visit comes after Trump posted a Truth Social post over the weekend offering White the press secretary position. He told reporters on Sunday that he was actually joking.

White told the room of journalists that he’s “always wanted to do this.”

“Who has the first question?” he said. “I have zero political aspirations.”

He said he was at a fight in London when Trump called him and told him he put the Truth Social post out.

“And the last 24 hours of my life has been insane,” he said. “Literally everybody, every media outlet was calling me, and I didn’t want to be disrespectful and say anything until he said something first.”

Trump said the social media post about offering White the position came after a “very bad press day.”

“I don’t know why I thought of his name. He’s been my friend for a long time. I said, ‘You know, I think I’m going to get Dana White to be my new press secretary,’” he said. “And I sent it to a group of the press, and that was it. I was really kidding. And then they wrote the stories as though I wasn’t kidding.”

White was asked if he had any advice for Trump about a proposed pardon for the deceased baseball player Pete Rose.

“I don’t advise the president on anything ever, but yeah, I think it’s fair,” White said.

Trump, after being told Rose had been convicted on tax charges, said he agreed.

“I think it’s fair to pardon Pete Rose,” Trump said.

“I think Pete Rose was very mistreated,” he continued.

Rose served five months in federal prison for tax evasion. Separately, he was permanently banned from baseball in August 1989 after an investigation found he bet on baseball games, including his own team, the Cincinnati Reds.

“He was gambling. He shouldn’t have done it,” Trump said. “But he went through 40 years of hell, and they never. And they should have given him a pardon. They should have given him into the Baseball Hall of Fame a long time ago.”

Major League Baseball reinstated Rose last year. It came after Trump had spoken to the commissioner about reinstating Rose.

At the end of the briefing, Trump asked White once again if he would like to be the new press secretary.

“Let me ask you the big question. Dana, would you like to be press secretary of the United States of America?” he said. “Look at the sign. You’d have this behind you all the time. The White House, Washington. Would you like that, or do you just want to stay with this ridiculous UFC?”

White thanked Trump for the offer but reiterated that he doesn’t want to be in politics.

“I am devastated to hear this,” he said. “Goodbye, everybody.”

articles.title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.summary: The US president said he spoke with Jensen Huang on Monday and asked him about the affair with the alleged spy.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology. The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off its value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.

Trump later told reporters at the White House that the FBI was looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the investigation, or when it was launched. The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.

According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.

Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday.

The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team.

The BBC has emailed Megaspeed several times for comment.

Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns.

Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy.

The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."

The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.

At the White House, Trump was asked several times, including by the BBC, when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.

Trump said he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.

"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added.

He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".

Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.

The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.

Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched.

Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear.

A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".

Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees.

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond

AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values

Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company.

Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.

It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today.

Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market.

articles.summary: Presented by CareQuest {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare PRESENTED BY The Big Story Feud exposes MAHA fault lines A public feud between former Health and Human Services adviser Calley Means and other Trump administration officials is exposing fault lines between the White House and the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement. © Natasha Kaiser In an…
articles.body:
A public feud between former Health and Human Services adviser Calley Means and other Trump administration officials is exposing fault lines between the White House and the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement.

In an explosive interview on the influential “Joe Rogan Experience” show last week, Means accused former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, James Blair and others of catering to special interest lobbying groups instead of protecting Americans’ health.

Means is a top ally of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and one of the primary architects of Kennedy’s MAHA movement. He resigned from the administration in October, just two weeks before the midterm elections. Means told Rogan he resigned because of internal opposition to popular issues.

“The simple reality in why I left is that there is a very concentrated group of people in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for and are, frankly, — I think it’s very clear — doing things for other reasons,” Means said in the interview.

Wiles and Blair, a top political adviser, both have denied Means’s allegations.

But Means is continuing to level broadsides against the two and other members of the administration. On CBS News’s “Face the Nation” Sunday, Means said he was concerned that Trump “has been subverted” by top aides and strategists who “treated him like a baby in many respects and used him.”

The extraordinary public attacks are coming days after Republicans suffered major electoral losses , spurring rounds of finger-pointing and internal debate about the future of the party and its leaders.

They are also exposing a rift in the marriage of convenience between MAHA supporters and the Trump administration, which happened during the 2024 presidential campaign when Kennedy dropped his own bid and endorsed Trump.

Many in the MAHA movement have expressed disappointment in the administration, with some even saying they felt betrayed on issues central to MAHA — the regulation of chemical additives in food and pesticides used on crops.

Some Democrats have been doing outreach to MAHA voters on the environmental issues they have some common ground on, and the growing disillusionment with the White House could put those voters up for grabs.

“There’s a lot of complicated issues that I’m sure Democrats are going to want to address. But when it comes to these issues on MAHA, I think there is huge opportunity in the next year to get some big things done,” Means said on “Face the Nation.”

The family of slain conservative activist Charlie Kirk said Monday it was “deeply disturbing” that the murder trial of his accused killer, Tyler Robinson, will not begin until summer of 2028 — nearly three years after Kirk’s death .

A Utah judge ruled Monday that the murder trial for Robinson, the 23-year-old man accused of fatally shooting Kirk at a Turning Point USA event at Utah Valley University, is scheduled to begin in June 2028. Judge Tony Graf set jury selection for June 21, 2028, and reserved 105 days for the trial, which will take place in Provo, Utah.

Kirk’s family criticized the trial date’s lengthy wait in a statement on Monday shared by Erika Kirk on social media .

“Today’s decision to delay the trial of the man accused of murdering our beloved Charlie until at least June 2028, is deeply disappointing,” the statement reads. “While nothing will restore the time we have lost with Charlie, every additional day without justice prolongs our family’s pain and forces us to wait even longer for accountability.”

The statement continues, “As we continue down this difficult road, we remain deeply grateful for the love, prayers, and support that have sustained our family through these painful months.”

Robinson’s attorneys sought to push the trial into 2029, arguing they needed more time to prepare their defense. Prosecutors had proposed a January 2028 start date, while Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, had urged the court not to delay the proceedings in an October hearing.

The judge said in making his ruling, he weighed the rights of both Robinson and Kirk’s widow in considering a trial date, and ultimately came to a compromise.

“This trial setting and case management order’s intent is to ensure that the constitutional rights of Mr. Robinson and Mrs. Kirk are upheld at every junction,” Graf said. “Each party is treated with the dignity and respect they are due, as they are human beings, and that the Sixth Amendment right is protected.”

Robinson has pleaded not guilty to charges including aggravated murder and felony use of a firearm. If convicted, Robinson could face the death penalty.

articles.title: Where all 18 unprojected House races stand
articles.summary: It has been nearly a week since the 2026 midterm elections delivered Democrats one of the biggest House majorities in decades — but some races have yet to be projected. While the outstanding 18 House races’ results won’t make or break the majority, both parties are hoping to squeeze as many seats as they can…
articles.body:
It has been nearly a week since the 2026 midterm elections delivered Democrats one of the biggest House majorities in decades — but some races have yet to be projected.

While the outstanding 18 House races’ results won’t make or break the majority, both parties are hoping to squeeze as many seats as they can out of the midterm election. Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) has projected 255 races for Democrats and 162 for Republicans.

DDHQ forecasts that Democrats will hold their biggest majority since the 1990s — 259 seats — while the GOP will clinch 176 votes in the lower chamber. Most of the races across the country were called on or soon after Election Night, but different states and localities count ballots in different ways and at different paces.

Here are the more than two dozen unprojected contests and the expected outcome once the votes are counted, as of Monday evening.

Republican Rep. Nick Begich leads in the returns and is on track to clinch a second term as Alaska’s at-large House member.

While Begich is up by 9 percentage points, only 71 percent of the votes have been counted in a state that uses ranked choice voting — which is only triggered if no candidate surpasses 50 percent of the vote.

Votes always take a long time to count in the sprawling state. Begich received 49.6 percent of the vote, meaning the race will likely head to ranked choice tabulation, which will be complete by Nov. 18. He faces independent Bill Hill, and the incumbent is the favorite to win the seat, with the contest “leaning” toward the GOP.

Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.) is looking to hold his seat against Democrat Johnathan Nez. With more than 95 percent of the vote in, Crane leads by more than 1 percent, avoiding Arizona’s automatic recount.

CNN projected Monday that Crane would hold onto his seat. DDHS has not projected the race.

The district voted for Trump by over 14 points two years ago, and DDHQ forecasted the contest leaned in Republicans’ favor.

In California’s primary system, the top two vote getters advance to the general election. That means two Democrats in California’s 4th District are facing off for the Sacramento-area seat.

Rep. Mike Thompson (D) trails Democrat Eric Jones, by 7,699 votes — but only 50 percent of the votes have been counted. 36-year-old Jones mounted a challenge against the 75-year-old Thompson, who has held the seat for decades, calling for generational change.

Nearby, Democratic Rep. Doris Matsui is also on defense, though the incumbent leads Mai Vang.

Matsui, as of Monday, leads her Democratic challenger by more than 10 points with 63 percent of the vote reported. She has served on Capitol Hill since 2005.

Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte (R), meanwhile, leads Democrat Tessa Hodge by 5,434 votes with over 95 percent of the expected vote counted.

The district voted for Trump by over 19 points in 2024, and DDHQ forecasted the seat was safely Republican. Obernolte won his reelection in 2024 by double digits.

In a Republican-on Republican and member-on-member matchup, Rep. Young Kim is trailing Rep. Ken Calvert by 13,241 votes with only 64 percent of the expected votes have been counted.

The pair of lawmakers were forced to compete in the same district after Calvert’s 41st District was essentially eliminated by Democrats when the party redistricted in 2025.

Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Col.) is currently on defense in the Centennial State. The firebrand lawmaker is trailing behind Democrat Eileen Laubacher.

Boebert is down by 3,237 votes as of Monday afternoon, and CNN projected the Democrat as the winner Monday afternoon.

The incumbent’s campaign said they are investigating “unusual voting patterns” and that they expect it to go to a recount. An automatic recount is triggered by a vote margin within half of a percentage point in the state.

An automatic recount is underwa y in south Florida where Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar is fighting to hang onto her seat.

Salazar, who drew the ire of President Trump earlier this year after she criticized his immigration policy, narrowly leads Democrat Elliott Rodriguez by less than half of a percentage point. DDHQ forecasted this race as leaning in the GOP’s favor ahead of Election Day.

Democrat Jake Johnson leads Rep. Brad Finstad (R-Minn.) by just 321 votes in the race that DDHQ predicted would “lean” toward Republicans.

Finstad requested a recount in the race, which should occur under Minnesota law.

“We will work to ensure that the full process established under state and federal law is followed, so that every vote is counted in an accurate and transparent manner as we move toward a final determination of the results,” Finstad said in a statement to Minnesota Public Radio .

In Minnesota, an automatic recount is triggered when the margin is within .a quarter of a percentage point.

On Long Island, Rep. Nick LaLota (R-N.Y.) leads Democrat Christopher Gallant by 6,677 votes with 93 percent of the vote counted.

The Associated Press (AP) called the race for LaLota, but it has yet to be called by DDHQ. The election forecaster predicted the seat would remain in the GOP’s hands.

Democrat Patrick Halpin is trailing Rep. Andrew Garbarino by 7,903 votes in New York’s 2nd District.

The “likely” red district, located on Long Island voted for Trump in 2024 by more than 14 points, is only reporting 85 percent of its expected votes. AP called the race for Garbarino but it has not yet been projected by DDHQ.

Rep. Greg Murphy (R-N.C.) holds a 233 vote lead over Democrat Raymond Smith — just 0.1 percent.

More than 95 percent of the vote has been counted, and his opponent is fundraising for a recount, per local media . Murphy was first elected in 2019, and he won is 2024 race by 55 points.

Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.) is at risk of losing her seat to Democrat Charles Hubbard as she trails by 99 votes with 90 percent of the expected votes counted.

Foxx, who has served since 2005, requested “nonpartisan election observers” to observe the count as it continues.

“At my request, nonpartisan election observers under the guidance of the Committee on House Administration will be present across the 5th District as the count continues, and will serve as important, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,” the lawmaker said in a statement.

Republican Rep. David Rouzer is also fighting to hold on to his seat — currently leading by 2,425 votes with more than 95 percent of the expected vote counted.

Rouzer claimed victory over Democrat Kimberly Hardy despite the race being too close to project by DDHQ. The election forecaster predicted the Republican was “likely” to win the seat ahead of Nov. 3.

Republican Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.), meanwhile, leads Democrat Colby Watson by 2 points east of Charlotte.

Ninety-five percent of the vote has been counted and the race has been called by AP, but not projected by DDHQ. Harris won by double digits in 2024.

In west-central North Carolina, Rep. Patrick Harrigan (R-N.C. )leads Democrat Ashley Bell by 3,029 votes — just over 1 percent with 95 percent of the vote tallied.

Harrigan published a lengthy statement to the social platform X after the election, calling the results “a reckoning” after Republicans lost the Senate seat and a number of House elections.

In a major upset, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tenn.) by 280 votes with 95 percent of the votes in.

DDHQ forecasted this seat as “safe” Republican, and DesJarlais won his election in 2024 by more than 40 points.

Rep. Michael Baumgartner (R) is expected to hold onto his House seat in eastern Washington, as he leads his opponent by 9,359 votes with 79 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ. The incumbent has claimed victory.

“A Democratic hurricane flooded across the country and this election victory is a testament to how hard we have worked for the people of Eastern Washington these last two years,” he wrote in a post to social media platform X.

Democrat Carmela Conroy said in a video posted to Facebook that the race was still too close to call and that the campaign is working to cure ballots.

articles.body:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) on Sunday vowed to deliver measures like raising the state minimum wage and protections for abortion following his party locking down the state House and Senate.

“We’re going to more than double Pennsylvania‘s minimum wage. Codify abortion rights into our state Constitution. Fund mass transit. Build more housing,” Shapiro wrote on social media Sunday afternoon.

“These are the commonsense things that Pennsylvanians want done. And with a Democratic trifecta, we will deliver on all of them,” he added.

Last week, Democrats locked down control of the Pennsylvania House, Senate and governorship. The wins came amid a larger blue wave across the country, with Democrats on the federal level also securing the House and Senate.

Those wins came amid rocky political territory for the GOP, with issues like the cost of living, President Trump’s sagging approval numbers and the war in Iran dragging Republicans down this election cycle.

A Democratic trifecta in the Keystone State is notable, considering Trump won Pennsylvania in the 2024 presidential election against then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump lost the state in 2020 against former President Biden, who has roots in Pennsylvania.

On Monday, Shapiro posted to social platform X a photo of himself at a wooden desk writing on piece of paper with the caption, “Pennsylvania, get ready. We’re just warming up for January…”

articles.title: US congressman files resolution to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth
articles.summary: Outgoing Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie calls on Congress to oust Hegseth over accusations of unlawful orders.
articles.body:
United States Republican Representative Thomas Massie has introduced a resolution to impeach US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war on Iran, strikes on purported drug boats and other alleged violations of US laws.

Reading from the text of the resolution in the House of Representatives on Monday, the outgoing Kentucky lawmaker accused Hegseth of carrying out unlawful orders and posing a threat to the Constitution.

Massie introduced the articles of impeachment as soon as the House opened for its first session after the midterm elections. Democratic Party leaders have pledged to investigate US President Donald Trump’s administration in Congress following their landslide victories in both chambers.

Massie reintroduced eight articles of impeachment against the defense secretary that he had first raised in September . Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson avoided a vote in the Republican-led Congress at the time by sending lawmakers home early.

In a news conference on Monday, Massie said he would welcome votes from any lawmakers who want Hegseth removed, even if they have not read the details of his bill.

“I understand that some of them just want to vote for this because they just want to see Hegseth gone,” he said. “I welcome their vote.”

He urged the defense secretary to resign before Democrats take control of Congress in January, predicting their investigations will include testimony from senior administration officials on how the Defense Department has been run under Hegseth.

Hegseth remained defiant, saying he welcomes the opportunity to defend his actions in Congress.

“There’s a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success,” Hegseth told reporters on Monday. “If we want to litigate” the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, he added, “I’m happy to do it all day long.”

He is expected to hold a news conference on Tuesday.

Hegseth accused of civilian harm, extrajudicial killings

Massie’s resolution alleges that Hegseth violated the Constitution by helping carry out the war on Iran without congressional authorisation, as mandated by the War Powers Resolution.

Hegseth “cultivated a warmaking culture” dismissive of rules of engagement that caused civilian harm, Massie alleges. He cited the US bombing of a school in Minab, Iran, which killed more than 150 people, including about 120 children, at the start of the US-Israel war in February.

The resolution also alleges that US strikes on alleged narcotics boats in the Caribbean and Pacific ignored mandatory safeguards and amounted to extrajudicial killings by Hegseth.

Other charges against Hegseth involve the abduction of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, suppressing free speech by restricting media access to the Pentagon and carrying out an unlawful war in Yemen against the Houthis.

Massie has been a frequent critic of Trump’s administration, particularly the Iran war. His outspoken nature has previously drawn anger from Trump, who backed a rival Republican candidate who defeated Massie in the primary elections earlier this year.

A majority of the 435-member House of Representatives would need to vote in favour of Hegseth’s impeachment. Two-thirds of the Senate’s 100 lawmakers would then need to vote to remove him.

While the measure is unlikely to succeed in the current Republican-led Congress, pressure is likely to mount on Hegseth when a new set of Democratic lawmakers, who won a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, are sworn into office in January.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker in January, said over the weekend that he supported Hegseth’s impeachment.

“The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran,” Jeffries said.

Although Democrats will hold the majority in the Senate, they are expected to have about 54 seats in the upper chamber of Congress – short of the 67 votes needed to convict and remove Hegseth.

Massie is also attempting to impeach Hegseth despite the objections of his own Republican Party, including from key leaders like Johnson.

“We don’t impeach Cabinet secretaries for political gain or for cheap tricks, and I think that’s what this is, and I think everybody knows it,” Johnson told reporters.

Trump administration officials have baulked at any attempt to impeach Hegseth, while simultaneously acknowledging the deep unpopularity of the war on Iran, which some have admitted likely cost Republicans the midterm elections.

“He’s guilty of two things, basically winning two wars,” Trump said about Hegseth on Sunday. “I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it’s awfully hard to say let’s impeach somebody who did that.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio also defended Hegseth, saying he has “done a good job” despite widespread criticism. Rubio also called the Iran war “necessary” while acknowledging that it was not “necessarily popular”.

articles.title: Após encerrar inquérito das fake news, STF avalia destino de mais de 100 procedimentos; relembre decisões | G1
articles.standfirst: Nesta segunda, o presidente do STF determinou o arquivamento do inquérito das fake news, aberto há mais de sete anos e que apurou ataques e ameaças a integrantes da Corte.
articles.summary: Nesta segunda, o presidente do STF determinou o arquivamento do inquérito das fake news, aberto há mais de sete anos e que apurou ataques e ameaças a integrantes da Corte.
articles.body:
A Presidência do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) ainda analisa qual será o destino de denúncias e relatórios da Polícia Federal ligados ao inquérito das fake news, encerrado nesta segunda-feira (9).

Um juiz auxiliar foi destacado pelo presidente do Supremo, Edson Fachin, para analisar quais providências serão adotadas em mais de 100 procedimentos que estão vinculados ao chamado "inquérito-mãe" .

🔎 O Inquérito das Fake News é uma investigação aberta pelo STF em 2019 para apurar a existência de notícias fraudulentas, falsas comunicações de crimes, denúncias caluniosas, ameaças e outros ataques contra o STF, seus ministros e familiares.

Entre esses casos estão quatro denúncias apresentadas pela Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR).

Três envolvem acusações de associação criminosa e tentativa de abolição violenta do Estado Democrático de Direito no contexto das manifestações ocorridas no fim de 2022, com bloqueios de rodovias, queima de pneus e impedimento à livre circulação de veículos.

A quarta denúncia envolve acusações de injúria e ameaça contra o ministro Gilmar Mendes.

Outra linha de investigação que permanece em aberto apura a obtenção de dados, a confecção de dossiês e a realização de ataques virtuais contra o general Santos Cruz, o então governador de São Paulo João Doria e a ex-deputada Carla Zambelli.

Sobre as denúncias, o STF precisa ainda decidir se os casos vão ser julgados pela Corte ou se vão ser encaminhados para outra instância.

Um caso que a PGR defendeu a continuidade é sobre uma investigação envolvendo o jornalista Luís Pablo, que mantém um blog no Maranhão e publicou reportagens sobre o suposto uso de um veículo oficial ligado ao Tribunal de Justiça do Maranhão pelo ministro Flávio Dino e familiares.

Luís Pablo foi alvo de uma operação de busca e apreensão autorizada por Alexandre de Moraes no âmbito do inquérito . A investigação aponta suspeitas de perseguição ("stalking") e monitoramento ilegal de Dino.

Na decisão que encerrou a investigação central, Fachin destacou que o arquivamento não impede o avanço de seus desdobramentos.

"Do mesmo modo, procedimentos investigatórios derivados poderão prosseguir quando apresentarem objeto certo, justa causa própria e autoridade competente definida. Para tanto, deverão ser formalmente individualizados, instruídos com os elementos pertinentes e encaminhados, conforme o caso, à Procuradoria-Geral da República, à Polícia Federal, ao órgão jurisdicional competente ou a outra autoridade com atribuição legal".

Segundo o ministro, "o encerramento ora determinado não constitui impedimento à apuração de fatos concretos cuja investigação permaneça juridicamente possível. O que se faz cessar é a continuidade do Inquérito nº 4.781 como procedimento originário, abrangente e indefinidamente aberto, atraindo a distribuição, por prevenção, da apuração de fatos novos supervenientes".

Ao longo de sete anos de tramitação, o inquérito das fake news acumulou decisões que ampliaram o alcance da investigação e provocaram controvérsias dentro e fora do STF .

Em abril de 2019, Moraes determinou a retirada do ar da reportagem "O amigo do amigo do meu pai", publicada pela revista Crusoé e reproduzida pelo site O Antagonista.

A decisão gerou forte reação de entidades de imprensa e juristas, que a classificaram como censura prévia. Dias depois, a determinação foi revogada. O episódio tornou-se um dos mais controversos do inquérito.

Ao longo da investigação, foram determinados bloqueios de contas em redes sociais, buscas e apreensões e quebras de sigilo de influenciadores e ativistas políticos.

Entre os casos mais conhecidos estão investigações contra Allan dos Santos, Oswaldo Eustáquio e outros influenciadores ligados ao ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL).

Em 2021, o então deputado federal Daniel Silveira foi preso após divulgar um vídeo com ameaças a ministros do STF e defesa de medidas autoritárias contra a Corte.

Embora o processo que resultou na condenação de Silveira tenha seguido um caminho próprio, a investigação teve origem no contexto das apurações relacionadas ao inquérito das fake news e seus desdobramentos.

Relembre as principais medidas adotadas ao longo dos sete anos:

Em 2019, foram adotadas, entre outras, as seguintes medidas:

pedido de informações à Secretaria da Receita Federal sobre o vazamento de dados envolvendo um ministro do STF, com determinação de afastamento temporário das atividades funcionais e oitiva de auditores fiscais;

busca e apreensão motivada por publicações consideradas ofensivas nas redes sociais e que incitavam a violência contra ministros do Supremo;

determinação para a retirada de reportagem publicada em site e revista que citava o então ministro Dias Toffoli;

nova busca e apreensão após postagens reiteradas nas redes sociais com graves ofensas ao STF e seus integrantes e, segundo a investigação, conteúdo de ódio e de subversão da ordem;

tomada de depoimentos de testemunhas para apurar possíveis questionamentos indevidos sobre condutas de ministros do STF em colaboração premiada;

pedido de apuração a Tribunais Regionais Federais a partir de relatórios técnicos produzidos após busca e apreensão;

quebra de sigilos bancário e fiscal para verificar a existência de esquemas de financiamento e divulgação em massa nas redes sociais com o objetivo, segundo a investigação, de atingir a independência do Poder Judiciário e o Estado de Direito;

abertura de inquéritos pela Polícia Federal no Ceará, Distrito Federal, Maranhão, Minas Gerais, Mato Grosso do Sul, Paraná, São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Rio Grande do Norte e Rio Grande do Sul;

pedido de informações a empresas de tecnologia sobre o envio de mensagens em massa por redes sociais e aplicativos;

busca e apreensão e tomada de depoimento em razão de postagens nas redes sociais consideradas ofensivas ao Supremo;

busca e apreensão após publicação em rede social que defendia o estupro e a morte das filhas de ministros do STF;

novos depoimentos e envio de dados à PGR para abertura de inquéritos; e

inclusão de relatórios técnicos e de inteligência elaborados pelo Departamento de Inteligência da Polícia do Estado de São Paulo, pela Polícia Federal e pela Secretaria de Segurança do Supremo.

Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) — Foto: Antonio Augusto/STF

Em 2020, houve quebra dos sigilos bancário e fiscal de pessoas e empresas supostamente envolvidas no financiamento e na divulgação em massa de conteúdo ofensivo ao STF e a seus ministros.

Também foram produzidos relatórios técnicos sobre a identificação de perfis no Facebook, Twitter e WhatsApp, obtenção de endereços de IP, solicitações a provedores e identificação de perfis automatizados.

Os autos receberam ainda relatórios de pesquisa sobre publicações em redes sociais com conteúdos contra o Supremo.

Além disso, foram realizadas novas operações de busca e apreensão, além do bloqueio de contas em redes sociais e da quebra de sigilos bancário e fiscal.

Em 2022, foi determinado que a Polícia Federal identificasse responsáveis e verificasse uma eventual relação com investigados nos inquéritos das fake news e da milícia digital.

Também houve tomada de depoimentos e análise de publicações do site "Movimento Direita Sul". O responsável foi identificado e dezenas de publicações consideradas ofensivas ao STF e a seus ministros foram catalogadas.

Uma manifestação apontou a existência de uma suposta organização criminosa com um núcleo financeiro e a finalidade de atentar contra a democracia e o Estado de Direito. O documento mencionava elementos de cinco inquéritos do STF e analisava o chamado "núcleo de financiamento".

Também houve decisão proibindo a publicação, promoção, replicação e compartilhamento de ataques e notícias fraudulentas.

Em 2023, foi determinada a remoção integral de anúncios, textos e informações veiculados e impulsionados a partir do blog oficial do Google com ataques ao projeto de lei conhecido como PL das Fake News.

Também foi determinada a remoção das mensagens enviadas pelo Telegram sobre a proposta, com fixação de multa por hora em caso de descumprimento e oitiva dos representantes legais da empresa.

Naquele ano, a PGR também cobrou um relatório sobre as investigações em andamento.

Em 2024, Moraes prestou esclarecimentos sobre as diligências realizadas e os diferentes eixos de investigação.

Em 2025, foi determinado o desbloqueio de diversos canais, perfis e contas em redes sociais.

Em 2026, o relator pediu que empresas complementassem dados sobre "campanhas pagas, publicadas entre janeiro a 01/01/2026 até 28/5/2026, em suas plataformas digitais (Facebook, Instagram e WhatsApp) que tenham como objeto o Supremo Tribunal Federal e seus Ministros".

Moraes também pediu à Polícia Federal dados sobre registros de entradas e saídas do território nacional.

Foi dentro do inquérito das fakes news que o ministro Alexandre de Moraes começou a apurar acessos e vazamentos de dados fiscais sigilosos de ministros do STF e de seus familiares.

A PF chegou a cumprir mandados de busca e apreensão contra servidores em três estados.

Moraes também decretou a quebra de sigilo bancário dos investigados com o objetivo de descobrir se as informações eram vendidas.

articles.title: Van Hollen ‘in listening mode’ on leadership run
articles.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who has been recently discussed as a possible Senate majority leader for his party in the upcoming Congress, said Monday he is “in listening mode” on taking up the role. “What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about…
articles.body:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who has been recently discussed as a possible Senate majority leader for his party in the upcoming Congress, said Monday he is “in listening mode” on taking up the role.

“What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we’re going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen told reporters Monday.

“And until then, I think that nobody should be making any commitments. But, in response to people calling upon me to step up here, what I’ve said on it is: ‘I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door,’” the Maryland senator added.

Last week, Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) reupped his push for Van Hollen to become Senate majority leader instead of current Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

During an appearance on “CNN News Central,” the Michigan Democrat reiterated his endorsement from earlier this year.

“I’ve been very clear: I think he’d be an amazing Senate majority leader,” El-Sayed told CNN’s Kate Bolduan on Thursday. “Of course, that’s a choice he has to make about whether or not he wants to pursue that.”

Adam Hamilton (Kan.), El-Sayed’s fellow Democratic senator-elect , on Sunday said that many people in his state saw Schumer as “polarizing.”

On “Meet the Press,” Hamilton was asked by NBC News’s Kristen Welker why Schumer, who Hamilton has previously critiqued, is not the right leader for Democrats.

“I mean no disrespect for Chuck Schumer,” Hamilton told Welker. “And I’ve told him that as well. But I think, at least where I live in Kansas, he is kind of a polarizing figure.”

articles.title: Trump defends Jensen Huang and Pete Hegseth at surprise news briefing with Dana White
articles.summary: The president said he would stand by the defense secretary if impeached and claimed, “We won the war in Iran,” despite ongoing conflict in the region.
articles.body: In his first post-midterm news briefing, President Donald Trump on Monday talked about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, the effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the massive Republican losses at the ballot box last week. Trump was joined at the impromptu briefing by Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White, to whom he jokingly offered the White House press secretary job last week. The president said he thought he would have “a little fun” by bringing White out to take questions from reporters. The president, who ended up fielding most of the questions, downplayed Rep. Thomas Massie’s push to impeach Hegseth. “He is a sick, sick guy,” Trump said of the Kentucky Republican who reintroduced articles of impeachment Monday that largely focus on the Iran war. “I will say this: The soldiers, the actual soldiers, the great people that do the work, the great patriots, they love Pete Hegseth,” Trump said while saying the secretary “won the war in Venezuela” and “won the war in Iran,” where peace talks have stalled and sporadic U.S. strikes are ongoing. “He’s done a very good job,” Trump said, adding that he would stand by Hegseth if he’s impeached by the House. A simple majority is required in the still GOP-led House for the articles to be approved and sent to the Senate for a trial. Only two Cabinet members in history have successfully been impeached; neither was convicted. Trump also defended Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Monday while revealing that he is under investigation by the FBI. People familiar with the matter told NBC News on Sunday that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang, the woman with whom Jensen Huang allegedly had the affair, was a Chinese spy. The two are not related. Trump said that he had spoken to Huang on Monday “just to see if he’s feeling all right.” “He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him,” Trump said, adding that Huang is a “very honorable man.” Huang said in a statement Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to my wife.” Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday it was “initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China denied involvement, calling it a “smear.” The president also responded to comments he made about his immigration policy during a “60 Minutes” interview that aired Sunday, during which he said his deportations had been “too tough,” and signaled a willingness to work with Democrats on potentially creating legal status for some immigrants. Trump said Monday that his policy “hasn’t changed” but that he’s “open” to an immigration deal with Democrats. “We’re not going to have amnesty or anything,” Trump said, without saying what, exactly, a deal might look like. “People are going to do it the right way. I have to do it. It’s unfair to other people, but certainly I’m open to it.” Trump also expanded on a Truth Social post from earlier in the day that questioned the midterm election results, despite his saying last week that he was willing to accept them. “I think the numbers were terrible in terms of those early votes,” Trump said when asked by reporters if he thought the results had been rigged. He then repeated his claim of foul play in the tight Alaska Senate race, which hasn’t been called. Trump concluded Monday’s briefing, where he spoke for a little more than 30 minutes, by jokingly offering Dana White the press secretary role one more time. “Thank you for the offer, sir,” White said. “I do not want to be in politics.” “I am devastated to hear this,” Trump responded before they both left the briefing room. The White House has been without a press secretary since late August, save for the five days Katie Zacharia served in the role last month.

articles.title: Crane staves off Democratic challenger in Arizona House race
articles.summary: Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.) is projected to win reelection in Arizona’s 2nd Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), defeating Democrat Jonathan Nez for the second consecutive election cycle. The race was close enough that DDHQ did not make its projection until a week after the election, as Democrats prepare to take over the…
articles.body:
Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.) is projected to win reelection in Arizona’s 2nd Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), defeating Democrat Jonathan Nez for the second consecutive election cycle.

The race was close enough that DDHQ did not make its projection until a week after the election, as Democrats prepare to take over the House next year with a larger majority than expected.

As such, the Crane-Nez race was a mirror to the rest of the country.

The Arizona race had become unexpectedly competitive in the final weeks of the campaign, with national Republicans pouring money into a district that President Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the race from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican” in October, reflecting the increasingly competitive political environment. DDHQ’s final preelection forecast also rated the district “likely Republican,” projecting a roughly 6-point margin in favor of the incumbent.

Crane, a former Navy SEAL and member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, has been a staunch Trump ally since first winning election in 2022. He was also among the Republicans who voted to oust former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.) in 2023.

Nez, a former Navajo Nation president , sought to make affordability and economic frustrations central to his campaign while also criticizing Crane’s support for the president’s agenda.

The Democrat previously challenged Crane in 2024, losing by roughly 9 percentage points, but he drew significantly more national attention and financial support in this year’s rematch.

The district covers much of northern and eastern Arizona, including Flagstaff and the Navajo Nation, where issues such as healthcare access, infrastructure and the cost of living have been central concerns for voters.

Crane’s victory secures him a third term in Congress.

articles.title: Trump downplays alleged spy plot targeting CEO who helped shape US tech policy
articles.summary: President Donald Trump downplayed revelations that close ally and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, insisting Monday that h...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump downplayed revelations that close ally and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, insisting Monday that he believed the tech billionaire's assertion that he knew nothing about the alleged espionage operation .

Trump's dismissal came amid growing scrutiny over the influential role that Huang played in advising Trump on AI and his approach to trade with China, even as the US government's intelligence agencies scrutinized the suspected spy who grew close to Huang in an investigation that played out for months behind the scenes.

"I really believe him," Trump told reporters during an impromptu White House press conference. "I think that he'll be in good shape."

The president's decision to stick by Huang marked the latest development in an extraordinary episode that has raised acute concerns about the economic and national security risks posed by the Nvidia chief's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy.

And it's likely to deepen Democrats' concerns over what the White House knew about the conduct of Huang and those around him — and why Trump nevertheless continued to rely heavily on the CEO's counsel in shaping the nation's multibillion-dollar artificial intelligence industry.

Senior Trump administration officials met earlier Monday with a group of top lawmakers charged with overseeing the nation's intelligence agencies, during which they discussed the intelligence surrounding Huang's affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based tech firm who is not related to the Nvidia CEO.

The private meeting with the so-called Gang of Eight was initially meant to focus on the war in Iran. But it came days after Jensen Huang admitted to the affair — and nearly a year after the FBI first raised worries to lawmakers that Alice Huang might be feeding information to China, two people familiar with the matter told CNN. (Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that the allegation that Alice Huang was gathering information for Beijing was "purely groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.")

Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, and CIA Director John Ratcliffe were spotted on Capitol Hill as Trump officials huddled for more than an hour with the Gang of Eight lawmakers charged with overseeing the nation's intelligence agencies.

But lawmakers indicated afterward they still had more questions than answers, with Democrats vowing a slew of investigations into the matter once they take control of Congress in January.

"The export of advanced semiconductors to China or countries where China might access them is a matter of immense national security importance," Rep. Jim Himes, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said in a statement. "We are aggressively pursuing more information to understand what happened and whether the decision-making process to export chips was improperly influenced or compromised."

Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and built it into one of the world's most valuable companies, is among a handful of tech billionaires who have played an influential role in shaping Trump's hands-off regulatory approach to the AI industry.

In September, the CEO helped craft a pledge that he and other major AI executives signed at the White House committing to "self-police" their companies. Huang has also repeatedly pressed Trump for greater freedom to sell advanced AI chips to China, putting himself at the center of one of the most critical and contentious debates within the administration.

"An amazing man, gotten to know him so well, Jensen Huang," Trump said last month as he awarded him the National Medal of Science. "The entire world is now running on Nvidia."

Huang's cozy relationship with Trump, including regular phone calls and trips to Washington for meetings in the West Wing, has persisted despite long-running suspicions within the government that he could be an unwitting conduit of information to China's government.

Federal agents first informed some lawmakers roughly a year ago that they suspected Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort," citing his close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen who represented the data center company Megaspeed.

The FBI officials noted that Alice Huang suddenly had an unusual level of purchasing power for someone in her position, one of the people familiar said.

Those initial suspicions formed the foundation of a classified memo issued in May warning that Jensen Huang had a close relationship with a woman the US now concluded was a Chinese spy, a US official and another person familiar with the matter said.

The memo was overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and circulated among a small group of senior administration officials before Trump's trip to China to meet with the country's leader, Xi Jinping, those sources said. Around the same time, a New York research firm that specializes in betting against publicly traded companies published its own report questioning the "uncomfortably close" relationship between the Nvidia CEO and Alice Huang.

Trump did not take any apparent action to distance himself from Jensen Huang. Huang was not initially among the tech executives and businessmen invited to accompany Trump on the China trip, though it's unclear whether that decision was tied to the Rubio memo.

And Trump ultimately insisted that the Nvidia CEO join him. Huang boarded Air Force One during a layover in Alaska, accompanying Trump and his top aides for the final leg of the flight to China.

The president later hailed him as "the Great Jensen Huang" in a social media post insisting that reports he was not invited were incorrect. "I will be asking President Xi, a Leader of extraordinary distinction to 'open up' China so that these brilliant people can work their magic, and help bring the People's Republic to an even higher level!"

Trump on Monday claimed he only recently learned of the concerns surrounding Huang, and was not aware of the suspected espionage operation when he brought him to Beijing.

The revelations have generated far more alarm among federal officials and others in Trump's orbit, who expressed shock that a suspected Chinese spy could gain such direct access to an executive running perhaps the nation's most important AI company — and potentially, by extension, decision-making at the government's highest levels.

"Jaw-dropping," said one former senior Trump official. "The stakes of that are just so high."

Two former senior intelligence officials at the FBI also questioned the decision not to provide Huang with a "defensive briefing" that would have informed him that he could be the target of Chinese intelligence.

Some Trump allies, meanwhile, have fretted privately that the question of what the president knew about Huang's affair, and when, gifted Democrats a potent opportunity to launch damaging investigations — and potentially form the basis for an impeachment effort that many in the president's orbit have come to see as inevitable after Tuesday's midterm elections.

Senior Democrats in both the House and Senate are already vowing to launch probes into the matter.

"The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt," Sen. Chris Coons, who is poised to lead the Senate Foreign Relations Committee next year, wrote in a recent post on X. "Congress will investigate and get answers."

Republicans have also sought information from Nvidia, in a sign of the distress over the prospect of China gaining intelligence that could give it an edge in its intense competition with the US to develop AI technology. A trio of House Republicans last week demanded that Huang sit for a confidential briefing this month.

"To me, the real damage goes beyond the attempted influence or the limited intelligence gathering on Nvidia's [intellectual property] that inevitably occurred," said Holden Triplett, who served as director of counterintelligence at the National Security Council in the first Trump administration. "It's all the small details she was likely able to collect about partners, suppliers, how sanctions work in practice, and potential workarounds."

Nvidia said it will conduct its own investigation into Huang's conduct, though it remains unclear whether the company's board is willing to fire him — and what repercussions that would have for the economy. There is no obvious successor to Huang, who has turned Nvidia into a powerhouse supplier of the chips at the center of the AI boom.

Huang's troubles have also generated fears throughout the broader sector among lobbyists and policymakers who worry the episode prompted renewed enthusiasm in Congress for more stringently regulating AI companies, dampening the gains that have driven the broader stock market consistently higher.

Yet despite the implications for national security, the economy and Trump's own administration, the president insisted on Monday that none of it much worried him.

"I'd certainly check with the intelligence people," he said of when he was first made aware of the concerns tied to Huang. "They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn't make much of an impact on me."

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN's Kylie Atwood, Katie Bo Lillis and Sean Lyngaas contributed to this report.

articles.title: New White House chief of staff Miller shuts door on big business
articles.summary: Under previous chief of staff Susie Wiles, many CEOs had a channel that helped them soften Trump administration policies or seek favors.
articles.body:
The replacement of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with her hardline deputy Stephen Miller shuts the door through which many CEOs softened Trump administration policies or sought favors, and sets the stage for more direct confrontation with business in the second half of Trump's term.

Even CEOs skeptical of Trump's chaotic style and his hostility to trade and immigration found that they could, with the help of Wiles and now-former tech czar David Sacks, talk Trump out of his aides' most disruptive moves, and beat back everything from worksite raids to canceling TSA PreCheck.

Former Robert F. Kennedy Jr. adviser Calley Means complained on CBS News Sunday that Wiles helped big business foil Kennedy's health plans. Now CEOs are unsure who to call, a top DC lobbyist tells Semafor — and aren't sure that Miller, whose career focus has been on stopping immigration, is inclined to take their side with Trump.

articles.title: GOP Rep. Lauren Boebert will lose reelection to Democrat Eileen Laubacher in Colorado, CNN projects
articles.summary: Retired Rear Adm. Eileen Laubacher, a Democrat, will flip Colorado’s 4th District, CNN’s Decision Desk projects, ending conservative firebrand Rep. Lauren Bo...
articles.body:
Retired Rear Adm. Eileen Laubacher, a Democrat, will flip Colorado's 4th District, CNN's Decision Desk projects, ending conservative firebrand Rep. Lauren Boebert's tenure in Congress.

Boebert's loss comes after she elected to run in a more conservative district last cycle in an effort to preserve her political future. But Laubacher, who served more than three decades in the Navy, capitalized on the national headwinds against the GOP and focused her campaign on affordability issues.

The win denies Boebert, an ally of President Donald Trump and one of the most outspoken conservatives in the House Republican conference, a fourth term. Boebert was first elected in 2020, after she upset a fifth-term Republican incumbent in a primary.

In that time, she has emerged as one of the most recognizable, and at times polarizing, faces of the GOP's MAGA wing, drawing attention from both Democrats and Republicans. Former President Joe Biden, whom she heckled during his 2022 State of the Union address, once billed her as "one of the leaders of this extreme MAGA movement." The 39-year-old has also been a source of frustration for Republican speakers Kevin McCarthy and Mike Johnson.

Speaking to reporters Monday night, Boebert did not concede the race and suggested she was looking ahead to military and overseas ballots still coming in.

"Hopefully, we'll have that number on Friday, and whatever decisions are, whatever comes of that, then we'll accept that and move forward in whatever way," she said.

Trump endorsed Boebert days before the election, praising her in a Truth Social post as a "MAGA Warrior, who has been with us from the very beginning." But the pair have also been at odds at times. She drew the president's ire earlier this year when she campaigned with one of his most vocal Republican critics in the House, Kentucky's Thomas Massie, in his primary. The appearance prompted Trump to call her "dumb" and "weak-minded" and he threatened to withdraw his endorsement.

Boebert also crossed Trump and House Republican leaders last year when she joined a Democratic push to force the release of the Jeffrey Epstein case files, resisting a White House effort to sway her vote. At the time, GOP leaders opposed the release of the files, citing the potential disclosure of the names of Epstein's victims.

This wasn't the first time Boebert faced a tough reelection fight. She won reelection in 2024 by over 11 points, but nearly lost her race in a different district in 2022. She beat Democrat Adam Frisch by only 546 votes.
